dossiers.title: Haruki does not merely meddle: he takes over and gets results
dossiers.claim: Across school, service work, publishing, and private crises, the Japanese defines Haruki through compulsive executive action: he assumes unassigned work, organizes people, prepares behind the scenes, and carries a problem through to an outcome. Todokanai TL repeatedly replaces that action with a personality label, a lecture, a sentimental motive, an attempted outcome, or a narrower job description.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The recurring vocabulary is operational rather than merely temperamental: 仕切る and 仕切り癖 for taking charge, 根回し for advance groundwork, 陰ひなたから支える for support both publicly and behind the scenes, 力ずくで見つけ出す for mobilizing others and actually finding someone, and professional milestones such as 初校 and being entrusted with an entire magazine. Even お節介 is repeatedly demonstrated through labor that materially changes another person's situation.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The English reader is often left with a nosy or preachy young man rather than an exhausting but effective organizer. The loss is cumulative: school duties become one invented office, quiet support becomes two-facedness, a successful search becomes an attempt, publishing authority becomes writing, and intrusive material help is repeatedly summarized as nosiness.
dossiers.limits: Meddling, nosy, and even reign of terror are sometimes defensible because the Japanese itself makes Haruki intrusive and overbearing. The dossier does not replace every お節介 with praise. It marks red only where agency, competence, result, role, or evaluation changes; one locally defensible 'nosy' line is included only as pattern support, and two preserved lines are included as counterexamples.

examples.note: Haruki names his compulsive habit of taking charge; the English changes it into enjoyment of cleaning up other people's messes.
examples.japanese: 「俺の仕切り癖を知ってて俺に振るお前が悪い！」
examples.todokanai: "It's your fault for throwing it my way when you know I enjoy cleaning up others' messes!"

examples.note: His practical refusal to leave a hole in the festival-stage program becomes a sentimental wish not to leave regrets onstage.
examples.japanese:
「何度も言うけど、そう言うんじゃないから。
ただ純粋に、ステージに穴を開けたくなくて。
…お前の言うとおり、学園最後の思い出作りだし」
examples.todokanai: "I've told you many times already, that's not how it is. I simply don't want to leave any regrets on the stage… I want to create fond memories of the last of my school days, just like you said."

examples.note: Setsuna lists several concurrent school duties; Todokanai TL compresses them into the invented title 'head of the festival committee' and shifts them into the past.
examples.japanese:
「北原くんは、学園祭実行委員とか、
クラス委員とか色々なお仕事を兼任してるので、
お世話になった方も多いと思います」
examples.todokanai: "In the past, Kitahara-kun was the head of the festival committee and he was also a class representative. He's been involved with a lot of things at school, so I'm sure he's had many opportunities to help you all out with all sorts of things."

examples.note: Setsuna praises Haruki for supporting the band publicly and behind the scenes; the English makes that support a product of his 'two-faced nature.'
examples.japanese:
「普段と同様、いつもわたしたちメンバーを、
陰ひなたから支えてくれる、
とても頼りがいのある人です」
examples.todokanai: "And just as he's done for many of you, he was the one driving us on and supporting us through his two-faced nature. He's someone that we could always depend on."

examples.note: Haruki recalls that he routinely handled classroom lockup; the English instead praises Koharu for remembering it.
examples.japanese:
「教室の戸締まりとかも、よくやった。
結構忘れてく奴ら多いんだよな」
examples.todokanai: "Remembering to lock up is pretty impressive. Most people forget all about it."

examples.note: Koharu calls him an incorrigibly good-natured do-gooder for helping strangers and people he dislikes; the English retains only 'obnoxious meddler.'
examples.japanese:
関係ない人間にまでお節介を焼き、
自分の嫌っている人間までも助けようとする、
救いがたいお人好し。
examples.todokanai: Worrying about complete strangers, and even going so far as to help out someone you hate. An obnoxious meddler.

examples.note: Being entrusted with production of an entire magazine issue, including editing, is reduced to being allowed to write one.
examples.japanese:
『新しいプロジェクトが決まった。
雑誌を一冊、任せてもらえることになった』
examples.todokanai: "My new project has been decided on. They're going to let me write an entire issue."

examples.note: First proofs due that day become a first draft, moving Haruki's project backward in the production cycle and diminishing the speed that amazes his coworkers.
examples.japanese:
「今日中に初校上がります。
週末にはこっちの作業は全部終わる予定です」
examples.todokanai: "I'll get the first draft finished today. As things stand right now, everything should be done by the weekend."

examples.note: Haruki says he repeatedly mobilized a large search and forcibly succeeded in finding Setsuna; the English says only that he attempted to find her.
examples.japanese:
その度ごとに、俺は周囲の人たちを巻き込んで
大規模な捜査網を引き、
雪菜を力ずくで見つけ出してきた。
examples.todokanai: Each time I involved everyone around me, and organized a search on a large scale in an attempt to find her.

examples.note: His efficiency rule minimizes new music across both album and concert; the English nearly reverses the production plan by forbidding overlap.
examples.japanese:
「手を抜いてるわけじゃない。効率化だ！
アルバムはもちろん、追加公演での新曲はなし。
いや、どれだけ譲ってもせめて１曲…」
examples.todokanai: "We're not cutting corners, we're making things efficient! The album I've thought of won't include songs you'll play in the additional concert, of course. Well, I suppose if you absolutely insist, we could at least include one new song…"

examples.note: Setsuna contrasts Haruki's constant unsolicited care for others with his dislike of receiving it; Todokanai TL reduces both sides of the character motif to lecturing.
examples.japanese:
「春希くんって、他人にはあんなにお節介なのに、
自分がお節介されるの嫌がるもんね」
examples.todokanai: "Haruki-kun, you insist on lecturing others, but you can't stand getting lectured yourself, can you?"

examples.note: Haruki learned a friend was struggling to meet living costs and forced an employment arrangement through the restaurant; the locally defensible 'nosy person' wording is not red, but it weakens the force and material result that define the recurring act.
examples.japanese:
そんな、普通ではあるけれど普段通りでない反応は、こと雪菜にとっては心地良いものであったけれど、残念ながら今の彼女にそれを認識する余裕はなかった。

「そういえばさ、女の子の制服可愛いよね、あそこって」

「まぁね、それが目当てで来る男性客も、それが目当てで働く男子バイトもいる」

「あはは…もしかして友近君もその一人？」

　何しろ雪菜は彼―友近浩樹が今からバイトだということも、そのバイト先も知っていたし、その後ろ姿を見つけたのも声を掛けたのも全て偶然でなかったから。

「よしてくれよ…単に紹介してもらっただけだって」

「紹介？」

「俺が生活費にまで困ってるって知ったら、それを聞きつけたどこかのお節介が無理やり店に話を通してくれたらしくてさ…」

「それは…お節介な人だね」
examples.todokanai:
His response—normal, though not what she usually received—was a pleasant thing for Setsuna, but unfortunately, she didn't have the capacity to be aware of that right now.

"Aren't the girls' uniforms pretty cute there?"

"Well, there are definitely guys who come in just to see them, and… guys who come and work there just to see them, too."

"Ahaha! …You don't happen to be one of them, now, do you, Tomochika-kun?"

She already knew that this guy—Tomochika Hiroki—was on his way to work, and where he was headed. The fact that she spotted him and called out to him wasn't coincidence in the least.

"Give me a break… I just got a referral there."

"A referral?"

"Yeah, apparently someone heard that I was struggling a little with living expenses, and took it upon himself to pass that along to the restaurant…"

"Sounds like… a pretty nosy person."

examples.note: Todokanai TL correctly preserves Takeya's admiration for Haruki's impeccable advance groundwork.
examples.japanese:
「何という万全な根回し。
やっぱり俺、お前のこと過小評価してたみたいだわ」
examples.todokanai: "The way you keep all your bases covered is just impeccable. Maybe I'm underestimating you after all."

examples.note: The joke that both Satou and the manager call Haruki's take-charge style a 'reign of terror' survives cleanly; the source does not portray his competence as uniformly benevolent.
examples.japanese:
…佐藤だけでなく、店長にまで
『恐怖政治』と言われた、俺の仕切りなんか。
examples.todokanai: …My "reign of terror," as both Satou and the manager so coin it.

dossiers.title: A dry, brusque peer voice becomes officialese and generic seriousness
dossiers.claim: Haruki's ordinary Japanese voice is casual, clipped, and often funny through mock gravity, self-correction, literal-minded pedantry, deliberately overbuilt setups, and linguistic correction. Across the work, Todokanai TL repeatedly replaces those mechanisms with formal judgments, generic explanations, or lines whose register and speech act no longer motivate the reply.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Haruki's jokes commonly span turns: he poses as though saying something once, corrupts a proverb, supplies the wrong datum after criticizing a question, answers a formula literally, or pedantically defends equations. The next correction or reaction supplies independent evidence for the intended mechanism.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The English often retains the topic while deleting the hinge, leaving a retort without a setup or turning Haruki's self-mockery into bureaucratic authority and intellectual superiority. The cumulative effect is a more officious and generically serious Haruki.
dossiers.limits: Not every formal English phrase is an error, and the dossier does not demand slang for its own sake. Findings require a changed speech act, broken callback, lost joke mechanism, or material register reversal; local casual counterexamples remain visible.

examples.note: Haruki tells Chiaki to formulate her question properly, then deliberately answers a weekday question with the time. Todokanai TL changes the correction to 'take a guess,' so her immediate defense of her wording no longer has a cause.
examples.japanese:
「人にものを尋ねるときはちゃんと推敲してからにしろ。
１１時だよ」
examples.todokanai: "You should at least try to take a guess before asking someone. It's 11 o'clock already."

examples.note: Haruki pretends he has only been meaning to tell Takeya something; the English says he has told him before and destroys Takeya's immediate retort that he says it constantly.
examples.japanese:
「前から言おうと思ってたんだけどな武也…
今日こそはハッキリ言わせてもらうぞ」
examples.todokanai: "I've told you this before, Takeya… so I'll spell it out clearly for you today."

examples.note: 'Listen and be amazed' sets up Kazusa's refusal to listen and therefore be amazed; 'Listen and shudder' changes both tone and callback.
examples.japanese:
「聞いて驚け。
なんとあの…」
examples.todokanai: "Listen and shudder! It turns out she's…"

examples.note: Haruki deliberately substitutes 'stupidity' into a fixed proverb about buying hardship while young; the English normalizes it into an ordinary maxim and strands Takeya's correction.
examples.japanese:
「それに…
『若いうちの馬鹿は買ってでもしろ』って言うだろ？」
examples.todokanai: "Besides, people say 'fool around while you're still young,' right?"

examples.note: He undercuts his own supposedly enlightened advice as absurd talk from teenagers; the English instead suggests their peers may be unable to understand him.
examples.japanese:
「そんな生き方の方が今よりよっぽど楽しいと思うけどな。
いや、まぁ俺らの歳でこんな悟ったようなこと言っても
しょうがないとは思うんだけど」
examples.todokanai: "I think living that way is a lot better in comparison. No, I guess I'm not sure if people our age would understand such a line of thought."

examples.note: A mock-presentational 'Then why? That's the question' becomes an answer to a question Setsuna never asked.
examples.japanese:
「だったら何で？　というわけだ。
わかった？　秘密兵器のボーカルさん？」
examples.todokanai: "That's my answer to you asking why. Got it, Miss Secret-weapon-singer?"

examples.note: Haruki jokes that if his brain learned of his painfully earnest line it would ban it from broadcast; the English turns the gag into a generic claim about not thinking clearly.
examples.japanese:
だって、こんな痛い台詞、
脳に知れたら絶対に放送禁止だ。
examples.todokanai: Because I know full well I'd never say something as embarrassing as this if my brain were working properly.

examples.note: His blunt reminder that Chiaki belongs to the seminar becomes 'Given that I'm in charge of you,' inventing a more officious personal authority.
examples.japanese: 「所属してんだから来て当然だろ？」
examples.todokanai: "Given that I'm in charge of you now, isn't that obvious?"

examples.note: Haruki accuses two coworkers of actively letting Koharu talk them around; the English merely orders them to say something and deletes the joke that silence is capitulation.
examples.japanese: 「お前ら言いくるめられようとしてるだろ！？」
examples.todokanai: "You two, why don't you say something!?"

examples.note: His internal reply to the formulaic 'thanks for your hard work' is the literal deadpan 'Yes... I'm tired'; the English makes him congratulate himself for working hard.
examples.japanese: はい…疲れました。
examples.todokanai: Yes… I know I've been working hard.

examples.note: A dry question about what kind of doujinshi operation expects one man to write, photograph, edit, print, and sell becomes a question about being self-employed.
examples.japanese: 「どこの同人誌ですか…」
examples.todokanai: "Do you take me for someone who's self-employed…?"

examples.note: His grotesquely comic threat that Kazusa's infected hand will rot and drop off at the wrist with a plop becomes the more generic image of pus gushing out.
examples.japanese:
「化膿するぞ？
腐りきって、手首からぽとっと落ちるぞ？」
examples.todokanai: "The wound will become infected, you know? It'll fester, and pus will gush out of your wrist."

examples.note: Accused of writing lyrics like equations, Haruki pedantically replies that equations are more functional and beautiful; 'a practical appeal to being formulaic' deletes the literal-minded joke.
examples.japanese:
「馬鹿言うな。
…数式はもっと機能的で美しいんだぞ」
examples.todokanai: "Don't be silly. …There's a more practical appeal to being formulaic."

examples.note: His teasing admission that he keeps using a clichéd pickup line because one fool always falls for it becomes a line about 'provocations,' stripping the married-couple banter of flirtation.
examples.japanese:
「そりゃ、いつまで経っても、
こんな陳腐な口説き文句に引っかかる馬鹿がいるからだ」
examples.todokanai: "I'm only doing it because a certain idiot keeps falling for the same old cliched provocations."

examples.note: Takeya's casual interruption about excluding the music program and reducing his imaginary total to twenty-one remains recognizably colloquial in English.
examples.japanese:
「やだなぁ、音楽科はパスに決まってんじゃん。
だから全部で２１人…」
examples.todokanai: "No way, I'd definitely pass on the music students. So that makes 21 in total…"

examples.note: Haruki's stammered concession that Kazusa is not his girlfriend is preserved without unnecessary formalization.
examples.japanese: 「そ、それは………そうだけど………」
examples.todokanai: "T-That's… true, but…"

dossiers.title: The same compulsion that helps people later overrules them
dossiers.claim: The interventionist tendency that drives Haruki's practical competence is repeatedly invoked when he assumes responsibility for other people's lives. In Coda, that same tendency can become control: he chooses burdens unilaterally, pushes through resistance, exploits loopholes, and instrumentalizes others while framing the action as care or responsibility.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Across periods, Haruki enters another person's circumstances, decides what outcome must be produced, and makes himself responsible for carrying it through. The later romantic material intensifies that recognizable structure, but each example is judged on its explicit agency rather than treated as proof that every act of care is coercive.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The translation repeatedly redistributes Haruki's chosen burden, turns active instrumentalization into passive suffering, factualizes the happiness he only hopes to provide, and erases the attachment behind procedural decisions. These changes soften or genericize the specific agency through which care becomes controlling.
dossiers.limits: This is continuity of a demonstrated behavioral tendency, not a claim that benevolence and coercion are identical or that later choices were predetermined. Correctly preserved self-restraint and overtly forceful closure are retained as counterevidence; the held motive passage is excluded.

examples.note: Haruki says a person cannot unilaterally declare the price paid unless the other person actually changes; the English substitutes the other person's acceptance, altering the principle he later violates.
examples.japanese:
「自分一人が落とし前をつけたって思ってても、
相手が変わってくれなかったら何の意味もない」
examples.todokanai: "Even if you think of paying the price alone, it will be meaningless if the other party doesn't accept it."

examples.note: His retrospective ownership—this is what I have done—becomes a future obligation, weakening self-accounting for the consequences he created.
examples.japanese: 「でもそれが、自分のしてきたことだから…」
examples.todokanai: "But that's just what I have to do…"

examples.note: Haruki vows that he himself will work, learn the language, and carry two people—no, all three lives; the English redistributes the burden among everyone.
examples.japanese:
「ちゃんと現地で仕事を探して、言葉も勉強して、
二人…いや、三人だって抱えてみせます」
examples.todokanai: "I'll make sure to find employment over there, I'll learn the necessary language, and the two of us… no, the three of us will bear it all together."

examples.note: He rejects sharing the burden because then he categorically could no longer choose Kazusa over Setsuna; 'might' hedges his explicitly selfish decision.
examples.japanese:
「………もし三人で背負ったら、
俺はもう、二人のうちからかずさを選べなくなる」
examples.todokanai: "…If we shared the burden among the three of us, then… I might be unable to pick Kazusa anymore."

examples.note: Haruki says he has used many people as stepping stones; the English replaces his deliberate instrumentalization with the passive suffering they caused.
examples.japanese: でないと、あれだけ多くの人を踏み台にした意味がない。
examples.todokanai: The amount of suffering we've caused to so many people would have been for nothing otherwise.

examples.note: The important truth is something Haruki absolutely must tell Setsuna; the English makes it something Setsuna absolutely has to hear.
examples.japanese:
「話があるんだ。
どうしても言わなくちゃならない、大事な…」
examples.todokanai: "I have something to tell you. It's something important, something you absolutely have to hear…"

examples.note: His justification remains conditional—if Kazusa can be happy, if she can smile beside him; the English turns his hope into certainty about what being with him will do for her.
examples.japanese:
「あいつが俺の側にいることで
幸せになってくれるなら。
隣にいるときだけでも笑ってくれるなら…」
examples.todokanai: "By being with me, she'll be happy. She'll smile for me just by being next to me…"

examples.note: Haruki's technical evasion of a no-contact rule becomes an assertion that he had to see Setsuna directly, replacing strategic boundary-lawyering with generic compulsion.
examples.japanese:
「ルール違反気味ってのはわかってる。
ただ、雪菜に直接連絡しなければって…」
examples.todokanai: "I'm aware that that's breaking the rules. I just felt like I had to see you in person, Setsuna…"

examples.note: He asks Kazusa to remain his burden for life so that carrying her will make him strive; the English preserves the motivation but omits the lifelong burden he is choosing.
examples.japanese:
「俺のために、ずっと役立たずでいてくれ。
俺が頑張れるように、一生、俺の負担になってくれ」
examples.todokanai: "Be useless, for my sake. Be my reason to work as hard as I can."

examples.note: Haruki was supposed to send Setsuna home immediately; the English says he wanted to, erasing the split between the plan he imposed and the attachment that made him postpone it.
examples.japanese:
「本当は、雪菜が来たとき、
すぐに帰ってもらうはずだった」
examples.todokanai: "The truth is, I wanted to send you home the moment you arrived here."

examples.note: The reason he delayed was that he could not bear to send Setsuna away; the English drops that attachment and leaves only abstract cowardice.
examples.japanese:
「それでも、雪菜を帰すのが今まで嫌で黙ってた。
勇気のない、意気地のない俺でごめんな」
examples.todokanai: "But I kept quiet about it until now. I'm sorry for being such a spineless coward."

examples.note: The English preserves Haruki's self-imposed restraint: public visibility lets him touch Kazusa, while privacy would leave him unable to stop.
examples.japanese:
だって、外だから…
誰かに見られるかもしれないからこそ、
俺はこうして、かずさに触れられる。
examples.todokanai: Because we're outside… It's precisely because there's a chance someone might see us that I can touch Kazusa like this.

examples.note: The English explicitly preserves Haruki taking little notice of Setsuna's thoughts and bringing the exchange forcibly to a conclusion; the early controlling edge remains visible here.
examples.japanese:
「嫌かな？　俺と帰るの」

「っ、そんなことない」

「それとも、余計なお節介がウザいかな？」

「それがなくちゃ春希くんじゃない！」

「…褒め言葉と取っていいんだよな、それ」

「あ、ごめん…」

　形式的に謝ってはみたものの、雪菜は自分の台詞が失言だったなんてまるで思っていなかった。

　ついでに、そんな自分の認識が彼を貶めているという可能性を考えたことも…

「とにかく、雪菜！」

「は、はいっ？」

「俺、やっぱり明日も迎えに行くから！　絶対に待っててくれよな」

「え？　え？」

　と、考え事をしている雪菜をよそに、春希が強引にまとめに入る。
examples.todokanai:
“Do you not like going home with me, or something?”

“N-No, it’s not that—“

“Or is it annoying, having me insist on helping like this?”

“If you didn’t, you wouldn’t be you, Haruki-kun!”

“…Should I take that as a compliment?”

“Ah, sorry…”

Though she apologized as a matter of form, Setsuna didn’t see her words as a gaffe in the least.

Nor did it occur to her that her own awareness of the fact might come out as a show of contempt for him…

“Anyway, Setsuna!”

“Y-Yes?”

“I’m gonna come and get you tomorrow, too! So you’d better wait for me.”

“Huh? What?”

Taking little notice of Setsuna’s absorption in her own thoughts, Haruki brought things forcibly to a conclusion.

dossiers.title: Setsuna's need, restraint, and private mischief are repeatedly recast
dossiers.claim: Across Introductory Chapter, Closing Chapter, Coda, and later stories, the selected errors repeatedly move specific moments of Setsuna wanting, asking, fearing imposition, restraining herself, or teasing in private toward stronger selfish, feigned, coercive, or exclusively self-serving agency. This is a demonstrated local pattern, not a claim that every aspect of Todokanai TL's Setsuna moves in one moral direction.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The Japanese repeatedly distinguishes needy desire from action: Setsuna wants contact, worries about its burden, suppresses herself, speaks from a publicly defensible position, and uses なんてね to expose private warmth or mischief beneath her perfect-girl persona. The script also gives her genuine calculation and cruelty; its force depends on keeping those categories apart.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: Todokanai TL makes the dependent grammar more controlling and the morally mixed grammar more uniformly culpable. The resulting Setsuna is easier to read as the calculating obstacle who forces, seizes, pretends, and acts only for herself, while the anxious need, consideration, private play, and wounded pride that complicate her calculations become less visible.
dossiers.limits: Setsuna really can be selfish, strategic, jealous, and cruel, and Japanese ワガママ can warrant 'selfish.' The claim is not that moral language should be removed. It is limited to places where the English adds fault, coercive agency, or feigned emotion absent from the source. Pattern-support examples remain outside the red-line ledger when the local effect is partly restored by context or falls within a defensible lexical range.

examples.note: Setsuna says there were many painful and difficult experiences at first, then separately apologizes for the awful things she said. The translation turns the suffering itself into painful and cruel acts she committed.
examples.japanese:
「色々とあったけど…
特に、最初は辛いことや苦しいことが多くて、
色々と酷いこと言っちゃってごめんなさい」
examples.todokanai: "So much has happened… Especially when it first started, there were so many painful and cruel things I did… And I also said so many awful things to you. For that, I'm sorry."

examples.note: Setsuna asks whether this side of her has put Haruki off or made him recoil. “Disappoint” makes her worry that she failed an expectation rather than that her intensity repelled him.
examples.todokanai: "…Did I disappoint you?"

examples.note: Setsuna makes the confession despite or at the cost of her embarrassment. Calling it 'shameless' reverses the characterization from overcoming shame to lacking it.
examples.japanese:
そんな雪菜の恥を忍んだ告白に、
俺は、限界を突破することで応える。
examples.todokanai: In response to Setsuna's shameless confession, I surpass my own limit.

examples.note: Haruki observes that under ordinary circumstances Setsuna herself might have made a slightly more selfish demand. The translation instead has Haruki judge her present, conspicuously considerate words as selfish.
examples.japanese: いつもなら、もう少しワガママを言ったかもしれない。
examples.todokanai: Normally, I'd consider her declaration a bit selfish.

examples.note: Setsuna peers into Haruki's face with concern or solicitude. 'Thoughtlessly' states the opposite attitude at the moment she cautiously asks whether he wants to see Kazusa.
examples.japanese:
いつの間にか神妙な態度に戻っていた雪菜が、
気づかわしげに俺の顔を覗き込む。
examples.todokanai: Setsuna peers at me thoughtlessly, now that she has finally regained her calm demeanor.

examples.note: Setsuna explicitly says she wanted the three of them to meet and wanted to reminisce all night. The English recasts her painful, frustrated desire as a neutral statement of what could have happened.
examples.japanese:
「三人で会いたかったのに。
夜通し思い出を語り合いたかったのに」
examples.todokanai: "The three of us could've met up together. We could've talked all night about our memories…"

examples.note: Setsuna asks to be allowed, for now, to speak from the principled or publicly defensible position and say only what is right. 建前 does not mean her anger is feigned.
examples.japanese:
「だけど、今は建前で怒らせて。
すごく原則的なこと言わせて。
正しいことだけ、言わせて」
examples.todokanai: "But right now, let me pretend that I'm angry at you. Let me admonish you with my principles. Let me say only the right things."

examples.note: Haruki calls Setsuna a 'villainess far too saintly': her excessive goodness enables his moral collapse. 'Misguided, yet virtuous' removes the deliberately accusatory saint/villain paradox and substitutes a different fault.
examples.japanese:
俺を甘えるだけの情けない男へと、
言い訳ばかりのずるい男へと堕落させてしまう、
聖女過ぎる悪女。
examples.todokanai: She's a misguided, yet utterly virtuous woman who's degrading me into a miserable man who only wants to take advantage of her. She's turning me into someone who will give her nothing but excuses.

examples.note: Setsuna says she kept the disposable warmer inside her clothes to warm it for Haruki, then playfully retracts the intimate claim. The English tells Haruki to put it in his own pocket and makes her embarrassment causeless.
examples.japanese:
「これ、使い捨てカイロ。
懐に入れて温めておきました…なんてね」
examples.todokanai: "Here, take this disposable heat pack. Put it in your pocket and you'll feel nice and warm… oh, what am I saying?"

examples.note: Setsuna feared that if she grasped the happiness within reach, she might let go of what was truly precious. Todokanai TL says she deliberately let go of the precious thing in order to seize what was offered.
examples.japanese:
「手に届くものを掴んだら、
本当に大切なものを手放してしまいそうだった。
だから、だから…すごく我慢したんだよ！」
examples.todokanai: "I willingly let go of what was truly precious to me so I could seize what was delivered to my hands. That's why… that's why… I've had to endure so much!"

examples.note: Setsuna says saving Haruki was not her only motive; she also wanted to satisfy her own desire. Todokanai TL turns the additive confession into an exclusive contrast—she did not act to save him, only for herself—making her self-accusation much harsher than the source.
examples.japanese:
彼を救いたいから、だけじゃない。
自分の欲望も満足させたかったから。
examples.todokanai: Not so I can save him, but to satisfy my own desires.

examples.note: Setsuna wonders whether Haruki's improvement means she has outlived her usefulness. Todokanai TL turns that fear of being no longer needed into an accusation that he is actively discarding her.
examples.japanese: 自分が良くなってきたら、わたしは用済みなの？
examples.todokanai: Now that he's gotten better, he's just going to cast me aside?

examples.note: Setsuna says that she must restrain herself until Haruki's exams end; the English says that she cannot 'force this on' him anymore, adding coercion and a history of it.
examples.japanese:
「試験終わるまでは、
自重、しなくちゃいけないよね？」
examples.todokanai: "I can't force this on you anymore until the exams end, right?"

examples.note: Setsuna worries that a girl who says she wants a call every day may disgust him; the English describes a girl who makes him call every day and 'always' acts selfishly.
examples.japanese:
「毎日電話して欲しいなんて…
そんなワガママ言う女の子のこと、
呆れちゃったりしない？」
examples.todokanai: "A girl who makes you call her every day and always acts so selfishly… Isn't that bothering you?"

examples.note: Todokanai TL accurately preserves Setsuna's concern that their daily long calls burden Haruki with a large phone bill; the considerate side of the dilemma is visible here.
examples.japanese:
『もう、切らなきゃいけないよね…
毎日こんな長電話してたら、
春希くんの電話代、大変なことになっちゃうよね…？』
examples.todokanai: "We should probably hang up now… If we have such long phone calls every day, your phone bill will be terrible, right, Haruki-kun…?"

examples.note: Todokanai TL renders Setsuna's なんてね as 'I'm just playing with you,' retaining the private tease and her quick apology after she sees that it troubled Haruki.
examples.japanese:
「…なんてね。
ふふ、ごめん。困らせちゃったみたいだね」
examples.todokanai: "…I'm just playing with you. Hehe, sorry. Looks like I really troubled you."

dossiers.title: Kazusa's dependency, self-abasement, and register are repeatedly flattened
dossiers.claim: Across the work, the selected errors and cautious pattern supports repeatedly reduce or redirect Kazusa's humiliating dependency, self-abasement, deliberate self-denial, rhetorical acuity, and changes of register. Some grant rational dignity or romantic confirmation; others substitute the wrong agency, metaphor, or emotional category. The common result is loss of volatility and precision, not a single uniform elevation of her character.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Kazusa's Japanese voice moves between clipped roughness, dry mockery, cultural and musical intelligence, severe self-description, childlike reliance, and pleas to be needed. Her metaphors make dependence spatial and bodily: floating weed survives on water, consideration becomes refusal, and utility is painfully distinguished from emotional necessity.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The English preserves a compelling tragic heroine but makes her cleaner. Love she considers degrading becomes proof of being loved; dependence becomes overbearingness or usefulness; deliberate retreat becomes failure to understand; resolute support becomes coldness; literary recognition becomes generic prose. That favors the dignified, validated soulmate over the embarrassing, volatile, and sometimes almost childlike attachment written in Japanese.
dossiers.limits: Kazusa is genuinely dignified, culturally acute, rough-spoken, romantically validated in some routes, and described through idealizing imagery. The claim does not deny those traits or require clumsy literal self-abuse. It concerns places where direction, agency, metaphor, or emotional category changes. The counterexamples show that Todokanai TL can preserve her self-mocking scale and the frightening durability of her bond.

examples.note: Kazusa's escalating parallel description culminates in an unmistakable adaptation of the cadence and wording of Miyazawa Kenji's Ame ni mo Makezu. The English conveys the component traits as ordinary explanatory prose but does not recreate or signal the literary echo that structures the characterization.
examples.japanese:
「非競争主義、脱落者ゼロ、一緒にゴール。
決して人とは争わず、いつも静かに笑ってる」
examples.todokanai: "You avoid competition, you make sure no one's left behind and that everyone makes it to the end together. You don't oppose anyone, always smiling quietly."

examples.note: 凛とした describes Kazusa's dignified, resolute bearing as she wordlessly tells Haruki to trust Setsuna. Calling it cold changes supportive confidence into emotional distance at the point where the three musicians coordinate without speech.
examples.japanese: その凛とした表情が俺に言葉以外で告げてくる。
examples.todokanai: That cold expression tells me everything I need to know.

examples.note: Haruki indicts himself as Kazusa's accomplice—literally, someone helping carry her end of the pole—in sustaining the strong facade. The English makes Kazusa shoulder Haruki's burden and calls her selfish, reversing both subject and moral judgment.
examples.japanese: あいつの片棒を担いでる俺に。
examples.todokanai: She just selfishly shouldered what was supposed to be mine to bear.

examples.note: Kazusa alternates between consideration and trying out selfish demands. Bare 'is indulgent' is ambiguous and conventionally describes leniency toward someone else, so it fails to state clearly that she is the one making demands.
examples.japanese:
気を使ってみたり、ワガママを言ってみたり、
雪菜のことを気にしてみたり、
雪菜を気にする俺を気にしてみたり。
examples.todokanai: She tries to be considerate one second, and is indulgent the other. She worries about Setsuna one second, and worries about me worrying about Setsuna the other.

examples.note: Kazusa marvels bitterly that a defective article like her could fall in love with an ordinary man like Haruki. The English reverses the direction and says Haruki came to love her.
examples.japanese:
『あたしみたいな、ピアノしか能がない、
他にはなにもできない欠陥品が、
お前みたいな普通の男、好きになるなんてさ…』
examples.todokanai: "The fact that a normal guy like you would come to love a defective person like me, who's so incompetent that she can't do anything other than play the piano…"

examples.note: Kazusa persists in a refusal she calls consideration or restraint: she knowingly tries to withdraw for Haruki's sake. 'Refuses to get a clue' instead portrays her as failing to understand his hints, reversing her awareness and motive.
examples.japanese:
俺がどれだけはぐらかしても、
かずさは遠慮という名の拒絶をやめようとしなかった。
examples.todokanai: No matter how much I try to change the topic, Kazusa just refuses to get a clue.

examples.note: Kazusa says that she has no credibility with Haruki in this exchange. The translation turns that relational complaint into an absolute claim that nobody ever trusts her.
examples.japanese: 「信用ないんだな、あたし」
examples.todokanai: "No one ever trusts me."

examples.note: Kazusa is 浮き草, a floating aquatic plant or duckweed, contrasted with Setsuna as a rooted tree. 'Tumbleweed' breaks the next lines' water-and-nutrient logic and substitutes an arid image for the source's aquatic dependence.
examples.japanese:
雪菜が樹木なら、かずさは浮き草だ。
地面に根を張って強く生きていくことはできないんだ。
examples.todokanai: If Setsuna is a tree that plants roots, then Kazusa is a tumbleweed. It's just not possible for her to extend her roots and live firmly.

examples.note: As floating weed, Kazusa can only live by taking nourishment little by little from the water itself while cut off from earth and world. The English makes her travel in search of water, continuing the erroneous tumbleweed metaphor.
examples.japanese:
地面と、世界と隔絶したところで、
水から少しずつ栄養をもらって生きていくしかないんだ。
examples.todokanai: She must find water to sustain herself little by little as she goes, separated both from the ground and the world.

examples.note: Kazusa asks Haruki to need her, even a little. 'Let me be of some use' changes her plea for emotional necessity into utility, precisely the reduction her painkiller metaphor has made painful.
examples.japanese:
「だから、せめてあたしの胸で泣いてくれ。
少しでも、あたしを必要としてくれよ」
examples.todokanai: "Then at least cry in my arms. Let me be of some use."

examples.note: Kazusa says Haruki has no sense or talent for being a human being. She deliberately casts moral judgment as innate artistic センス, then extends the conceit through talent, artists, and Japanese people. 'Lacks common sense' turns this into conventional social judgment and breaks the sustained analogy.
examples.japanese:
「あいつの言ってることは全部間違いだ。
だってあいつは、人としてのセンスがないから」
examples.todokanai: "Everything that comes out of his mouth is wrong. After all, that guy lacks common sense."

examples.note: The narration contrasts Kazusa's extreme shyness with strangers against the inward-facing intensity that becomes conspicuous once she and Haruki are alone. Repeating 'extreme introversion' misses that private reversal and does not fit the force she directs toward him in private.
examples.japanese:
…おかげで二人きりになった後の内向的な激しさが、
ますます際立っていくことになる訳だけど。
examples.todokanai: …Thanks to that, her extreme introversion will become even more prominent when we're alone together.

examples.note: Kazusa calls herself a mother-fixated fool who goes trotting after Youko again the moment she is shown a little kindness; the English says Youko rationally 'regained my trust.'
examples.japanese:
「三年前に捨てられたくせに、
ちょっと甘い顔されるとホイホイついてくって、
あたしも大概マザコンだとは思うんだけどね」
examples.todokanai: "She abandoned me for three years, but with a few sweet words, she regained my trust. Looks like I have a bit of a mother complex after all, huh."

examples.note: Kazusa calls her continued dependence after rejection painfully embarrassing or cringingly pathetic; the English calls her 'overbearing,' moving the fault from inward humiliation to outward pressure.
examples.japanese:
「ふられたのに、捨てられたのに、
こんなに依存して、あたしって痛いだろ？
死んじまえってレベルだろ？」
examples.todokanai: "I was rejected, I was discarded, yet I'm still this reliant on you. I'm so overbearing, aren't I? Enough to make you wish I was dead, right?"

examples.note: Todokanai TL preserves Kazusa's terrifying temporal calculation: five years apart became almost nothing, so even ten years might be overcome.
examples.japanese:
俺たちの間の五年なんて、ないも同然だった…
十年なら、平気で乗り越えてしまうかもしれない。
examples.todokanai: These past five years apart might as well not have happened… We might actually be able to overcome ten years with ease.

examples.note: Todokanai TL preserves Kazusa's reluctant, self-mocking numerical scale, moving Haruki only from an average five to five-and-a-half or six.
examples.japanese:
「見直されたくなかったら、周囲と同化して埋没した方がよっぽど効果的だぞ」

「なにそれ？」

　―けれど、もしかしたらほんの少しだけ平均より上かもしれない。

　　七人並み、八人並みくらいは行ってるかもしれない。

「ほら、『不良が猫に餌やってた』とかいう落差による高評価がなくなるから、みんな普通に評価してくれるだろ？」

「あたしは誰にも評価されるつもりはない」

　―その証拠に、見とれたりはしないけれど、ずっと間近で見ていても苦にならない。

　　このまま見つめ続けていても、多分…
examples.todokanai:
"If you don't want people to reevaluate their opinion of you, just going along with the flow would work out better, you know."

"What are you saying?"

But, maybe he's just a tiny bit above average.

Maybe he's like a 5.5, or a 6, instead of just a 5.

"Look, that way people wouldn't be so impressed when you give a rare display of good conduct and evaluate you more normally, right?"

"I have no intention of letting anyone evaluate me."

As proof, I might not be captivated by him, but looking at him up this close isn't terrible, either.

dossiers.title: The triangle's roles, rankings, and culpability are repeatedly altered
dossiers.claim: Repeated errors alter who loves whom, who is first, who acts, who relinquishes a claim, and whether the three-person relationship is a demand, refuge, or impossibility. The mistakes are not one-directional, but together they make the explicit topology of simultaneous loves and distributed culpability less stable than it is in Japanese.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The Japanese carefully distinguishes liking from loving and 'number one' from exclusive love; present reality from wished-for lies; prior emotional claim from current relationship status; asking the other two to preserve the trio from privately seeking a pair; and being unable to act from choosing not to. Repeated labels and physical actions carry those distinctions across routes.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: Todokanai TL repeatedly converts partitions into rankings, rankings into exclusivity, current love into past love, and singular acts into mutual or future conditions. This redistributes moral weight: Kazusa gains stronger ownership and romantic confirmation, her failures become incapacity, Setsuna's position becomes less secure, and Setsuna's own contradictory effort to preserve three while pursuing two becomes either softened or unintelligible.
dossiers.limits: The source itself repeatedly presents Kazusa as Haruki's first love and Setsuna as the person who intervened; it also condemns all three. Some listed errors soften Setsuna's guilt rather than intensify it. This dossier therefore alleges cumulative redistribution, not a single conspiracy of direction. The two counterexamples show Todokanai TL preserving both the structural impossibility of returning from three to two and the shared knowledge of wrongdoing.

examples.note: The Japanese pointedly gives Kazusa and Setsuna different marked labels: 'that one' leaves, while 'the girl and I' remain. Todokanai TL renders both women as the identical quoted 'she,' erasing the hierarchy and making the quotation marks meaningless.
examples.japanese:
『あいつ』は去った。
そして、『俺とあの娘』だけが残った。
examples.todokanai: "She" is gone now. And only "she and I" remain.

examples.note: The quoted 『あいつ』 deliberately recalls Haruki's marked designation of Kazusa at line 20. Rendering it as generic quoted 'she' removes the echo and the contrast with Setsuna, even as Setsuna is holding him.
examples.japanese:
そんな瞬間も、俺の頭の中を占めているのが、
『あいつ』のことしかないって事実に。
examples.todokanai: Even at this very moment… I can't deny the truth that "she" is the only thing on my mind right now.

examples.note: Setsuna says she took Haruki and made him no longer Kazusa's, explicitly framing her act as theft from a prior claim. The English changes this to Kazusa's future inability to have him, weakening Setsuna's confession of guilt and the presupposed emotional ownership.
examples.japanese:
「わたし…春希くん取っちゃったんだよ？
冬馬さんのものじゃ、なくしちゃったんだよ？」
examples.todokanai: "I've taken Haruki-kun away, you know? You won't be able to have him for yourself, Touma-san, you know?"

examples.note: Haruki answers in the present: he loves Setsuna and has remained in love with her. The English changes both clauses to past love, erasing the deliberately cruel paradox that he still loves her while choosing someone else.
examples.japanese:
「好きだよ…
ずっと、好きなままだよ…っ」
examples.todokanai: "Of course I loved you… I've always loved you all this time…"

examples.note: Setsuna herself tears apart the hands that joined them, demonstrating the strength required to complete the breakup for Haruki's sake. The English makes the separation mutual and gentle, erasing her singular agency and the violence of the image.
examples.japanese:
俺たちが繋げていた手を、
自分から引きちぎってみせる。
examples.todokanai: We willingly shift our tightly intertwined hands away from each other.

examples.note: Kazusa warns Haruki about abandoning the person he has loved continuously for five years: Setsuna. The translation makes Setsuna the one who has loved Haruki, reversing the subject and weakening Kazusa's insistence that his own love remains.
examples.japanese:
「だから、そんなことしてしまったら…
五年間もずっと愛してきた相手を捨ててしまったら…
お前、一生後悔して生きていくことになるんだぞ？」
examples.todokanai: "If you do this… If you abandon the person who has loved you so earnestly for five years, you'll regret it for the rest of your life."

examples.note: Kazusa asks for lies that he likes her, loves her, and has felt unchanged since long ago. She does not ask him to rank her above everyone else; that added superlative destabilizes the carefully partitioned Setsuna/Kazusa arrangement.
examples.japanese:
「あたしのこと好きだって、愛してるって、
ずっと昔から、変わらぬ気持ちのままだって…」
examples.todokanai: "If you were to tell me that you love me, that you love me more than anyone else, that your feelings for me haven't changed one bit…"

examples.note: Kazusa grounds her safety in a present reality where Haruki loves Setsuna and an everyday life where Haruki does not love Kazusa. The translation turns the first into future ability and loses the explicit reality-versus-daily-life partition.
examples.japanese:
「雪菜のことを愛してる春希が現実にいるから。
あたしのことを愛してない春希が日常にいるから」
examples.todokanai: "Because you'll still be able to love Setsuna. Because there'll still be a you who doesn't love me."

examples.note: Kazusa says Haruki liked Setsuna five years ago and that she knows because she watched him. 'You're the one he's truly loved' adds both singular 'the one' and 'truly,' suggesting an exclusivity the source does not state before the following discussion of who remained number one.
examples.japanese:
「あいつは五年前から雪菜のことが好きだったよ。
ずっとあいつを見てたあたしだからわかるんだよ…」
examples.todokanai: "You're the one he's truly loved since five years ago, Setsuna. I know that full well because I've been watching him all that time…"

examples.note: Setsuna says Haruki's number one had remained unchanged throughout that period. The English turns this retrospective observation into a permanent prediction that she will never become number one, immediately clashing with her next statement that her best was to draw level and Kazusa's answer that Setsuna ultimately did become the woman he loves most.
examples.japanese:
「それでも、彼の中の一番はずっと変わらなかった。
…途中からだけど、ずっと彼を見てるわたしならわかる」
examples.todokanai: "Even so, I'll never be able to become the one he loves most. …I know because I've always watched him, even if not for as long as you."

examples.note: Kazusa says Setsuna made the effort that she herself did not make. The English changes self-reproach for not acting into inability, mitigating the agency and responsibility on which Kazusa bases her concession of defeat.
examples.japanese:
「でも雪菜は努力した。
…あたしのしなかった努力をさ」
examples.todokanai: "But you worked really hard, Setsuna. …You worked really hard while I couldn't."

examples.note: Youko asks whether anyone would go this far for a woman her boyfriend rejected who is now making a pass at that boyfriend. The English says Kazusa is trying to 'take back' the man she loves, granting her prior ownership and removing Setsuna's relationship boundary.
examples.japanese:
「普通、ここまでする？
ふった女のために。
自分の彼にコナかけてくる女のために」
examples.todokanai: "Would someone usually go so far? For a girl you rejected… for a girl who's trying to take back the man she loves?"

examples.note: Setsuna addresses Haruki: Kazusa is his eternal goddess, and he worships her enough to make Setsuna jealous. The English changes the omitted subject to Setsuna and says she too worships Kazusa, replacing romantic jealousy with shared devotion.
examples.japanese:
「永遠の女神、だよね…
悔しいくらい、崇拝してるもんね」
examples.todokanai: "Your eternal goddess, right…? It's frustrating to say, but I worship her too."

examples.note: Setsuna confesses the contradiction plainly: while asking the other two to preserve the trio, she herself sought to be alone with Haruki. The first translated sentence is nonsensical and duplicates the second instead of stating what she demanded of Haruki and Kazusa.
examples.japanese:
「三人でいることを二人に求めておきながら、
自分は彼と二人になることを求めた。
…かずさのこと、出し抜いた」
examples.todokanai: "I sought to become two amongst the three of us… I wanted to become two with him. …And I ended up stealing the march on you, Kazusa."

examples.note: Todokanai TL preserves the structural cost of accepting the trio: once all three are admitted, Haruki can no longer return to a two-person relationship with either woman.
examples.japanese:
それでも無理やり三人でいることを選んだら、
二度と二人に戻ることができなくなってしまう。
examples.todokanai: Even so, if I were to force myself to accept the three of us being together, I won't be able to return to just the two of us ever again.

examples.note: Todokanai TL preserves that Haruki and Kazusa both knew their earlier act was despicable and nevertheless did not stop, retaining shared culpability rather than assigning the wrong to only one participant.
examples.japanese:
だって、五年前の俺たちも…
互いに『最悪のこと』ってわかってて、
それでも止まらなかっただけ、なんだから。
examples.todokanai: Because even five years ago… we both knew we were doing something despicable. We merely didn't stop in spite of that.

dossiers.title: Malformed sentences, stock substitutions, and flattened rhetoric
dossiers.claim: Todokanai TL's English is not uniformly poor, but it has a recurring flattening tendency: concrete images, character-specific register, rhetorical structures, and comic mechanisms are replaced by explanatory abstraction or stock English, while literalized idioms and unresolved syntax sometimes produce defective sentences. Across a work whose characterization is carried by diction, rhythm, self-correction, and repeated figures, those choices cumulatively make the prose flatter even when the rough event remains recognizable.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Maruto's scripts repeatedly make form do semantic work: a character corrects a sentence halfway through, repeats a loaded word, extends an image across later lines, shifts register for a joke, or lets clause rhythm reveal hesitation and self-deception. The source therefore cannot be represented fully by transferring only the line's broad informational gist.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The recurrent result is English that explains instead of enacts, moralizes instead of preserving a character's exact self-description, substitutes generic idioms for scene-specific images, or burdens dialogue with abstract noun phrases. In the strongest cases the English is ungrammatical or incoherent; in the softer cases it remains understandable but loses voice, rhythm, or payoff.
dossiers.limits: This dossier does not treat brevity, literalness, or difference from another translation as proof of error. The twenty-one confirmed examples below are independently source-grounded public findings. Four further examples are labeled pattern_support because their English is defensible in meaning but illustrates a cumulative stylistic habit; they are not proposed as red-line errors. The four counterexamples show that Todokanai TL can write concise, effective English and that the claim is a recurring tendency rather than a universal verdict.
dossiers.diagnostic: “the fact that” appears on 445 mapped lines (466 literal occurrences) across 147 of 244 mapped scripts (76,557 mapped lines). This count is diagnostic, not dispositive. Many individual occurrences are grammatical and justified. Its value is to establish that fact-nominalization is a genuine corpus-wide house habit, after which the four non-red examples below show how the habit can weigh down otherwise straightforward clauses.

examples.note: The snow opens a white world before them and strands them inside it. An expanding world cannot leave them 'in its wake'; the English reverses the spatial relation at the climax of the cold open.
examples.section: Malformed or incomplete English
examples.japanese:
ただ白く、綺麗なだけの世界を目の前に広げ、
俺たちを、そこに置き去りにしてくれる。
examples.todokanai: A white world abundant only in beauty expands before our eyes, leaving us there in its wake.

examples.note: The comma splits the subject from its verb, while 'I'm pretty sure' never receives a coherent complement. Setsuna's hesitant apology becomes ungrammatical rather than hesitant.
examples.section: Malformed or incomplete English
examples.japanese:
「その、今さらこんなこと言うの、
本当に申し訳ないって思うんですけど…」
examples.todokanai: "Listen, I'm pretty sure saying this right now, seems really inexcusable…"

examples.note: Koharu concludes that the person on the recording is the same Haruki she saw in the music room. The English supplies neither a grammatical question nor the recognition, leaving the character insight unfinished.
examples.section: Malformed or incomplete English
examples.japanese: 「あの時の、音楽室の、あいつだよ…」
examples.todokanai: "Is the person I saw in the music room back then…"

examples.note: The source reaches its main predicate: Miyoko is now peering at Haruki with intense awkwardness. The English ends on a comma after a subordinate description, omits the present look, and never supplies a main predicate.
examples.section: Malformed or incomplete English
examples.japanese:

決して人とは争わず、いつも静かに笑ってる」
examples.todokanai: "You avoid competition, you make sure no one's left behind and that everyone makes it to the end together. You don't oppose anyone, always smiling quietly."

examples.todokanai: "I'll lend you my shoulder as well. If it's only for crying anyway…"

ちょっとした残酷な友情じゃんか～」

お前のこと、犯してるんだから」
examples.todokanai: "Of course I have… I'm about to make you mine, after all."

こうして大学進学を目指す生徒たちがそこそこに集う。

examples.section: A cumulative habit of fact-nominalization and clause stacking
examples.japanese:
「病気のこと、とっくに本人にバレてるのに、
誰もがそんなことわかってるのに、
それでもかずさの言う『家族』を演じるんだと思う」

examples.note: The lights themselves show that the darkness is a structure. The English instead routes the perception through an abstract 'becomes clear ... by the fact that' frame; understandable, but representative of the distancing cadence.

examples.japanese:
窓の外は、かずさが夜と誤解するくらい真っ暗だったけど、
周期的に目に入るかすかな灯りが、
その景色が人口の建造物であることを示している。
examples.todokanai: It's certainly dark on the other side of the window, which is why Kazusa thought it was nighttime, but it becomes clear that this scenery is artificial by the fact that we can see lights periodically flash by.

examples.japanese: 「小春希」
examples.todokanai: "Mini-Haruki."

examples.note: A Japanese preparation proverb is replaced by a natural English proverb that preserves its function and supports Kazusa's follow-up. This is exactly the kind of nonliteral idiom replacement the dossier endorses.
examples.section: Counterexamples and limits
examples.japanese:
「備えあれば憂いなし。
俺もたまにはいいこと言うだろ？」
examples.todokanai: "By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail. I say some pretty cool things sometimes, huh?"

examples.note: The line remains concise while preserving the joke that Io and Takeya's rotten bond has decomposed over six years and vanished without a trace.

examples.japanese:
「六年経つと、
腐った後に分解されて、跡形もなくなるけどね」
examples.todokanai: "That bond's as good as rotten and gone without a trace after these six years, though."

examples.note: Localizing ブラック as 'sweatshop' preserves the exploitative-workplace joke and lets the group escalate it naturally. The exchange demonstrates that strong domestication and lively English are compatible with fidelity.
examples.section: Counterexamples and limits
examples.japanese:
「ホント期待してるからね小春っち。何しろ最近のウチ、その“ただのアルバイト”が一週間続いたことないんだよねぇ」

「そういうこと言うのやめてよ鈴木さん。それだとウチがまるでブラックみたいじゃん」

「何言ってんだ松岡、ブラックでない出版社が生き残ってる訳ないだろこの出版不況のご時世に」

「木崎さんもさらっと肯定しちゃったらマズいでしょ……」

“We’ve got high hopes for you, Kohacchi. Lately, none of our part-timers have stuck around for more than a week…”

“Don’t say stuff like that, Suzuki-san. You’ll make us sound like a sweatshop.”

“What are you talking about, Matsuoka? In times like these, with publications in such a slump, no publishing company could survive without being a sweatshop.”

“Do you have to affirm that so readily, Kizaki-san…?”

But, well, whether it was because they were more experienced members of society as her seniors, or whether they were all just completely irresponsible, the others present let her formal attitude wash right off of them and got swept up in their own lively conversations.

dossiers.title: Who acts, feels, or bears the consequence
dossiers.claim: Across school, work, romance, and sex scenes, Todokanai TL repeatedly assigns an action, interpretation, injury, or responsibility to a different participant from the one established by the Japanese. These are not cosmetic pronoun choices: they change who visits, decides, desires, betrays, suffers, controls an action, or understands another person.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Japanese often omits a subject once viewpoint and turn structure establish it, but case relations, transitivity, quoted speech, and adjacent reactions still constrain the agent, patient, and experiencer. The selected cases span explicit passive/causative relations, requests whose actor is recoverable from the threatened action, and interior narration whose viewpoint fixes whose feeling is being described.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The cumulative result redistributes characterization and culpability. Haruki's guilt can become Kazusa's failure; Mari's injury can become Haruki's; Setsuna's interpretation can become Haruki's declaration; and desire flowing toward one lover can be reversed into possession of her. A reader following only the English receives a different causal and psychological scene.
dossiers.limits: Omitted subjects are not automatically ambiguous or mistranslated, and natural English may name a participant Japanese leaves implicit. A finding is included only where local grammar and context fix the relation and the English changes it. The two counterexamples show defensible subject recovery and a scene in which shared culpability remains shared.

examples.note: Haruki says he has just visited Kazusa's lodging; the English invents Kazusa returning there and reverses the visitor.
examples.japanese:
「あれぇ？　おかしいなぁ…
つい先ほど滞在先に伺ってきたばかりなんですが」
examples.todokanai: "Huh? That's strange… I swear she just came back to her residence."

examples.note: Mari let Haruki take her while concealing her transfer; the English makes Mari the one who embraced him, reversing the sexual agency.
examples.japanese:
異動のことをずっと黙ったまま、
俺に抱かれた…？
examples.todokanai: She willingly embraced me while being silent about her impending transfer all the while…?

examples.note: Haruki blames his own failure to worry; the English assigns that failure to Kazusa and redirects his guilt.
examples.japanese: けどあの時、特別に心配しなかったせいでお前は…
examples.todokanai: But thanks to you not worrying about it back then, the result was…

examples.note: Haruki insists Mari must have been shocked; the English makes Haruki himself newly feel shocked.
examples.japanese: 絶対に、ショックだったに決まってる。
examples.todokanai: Now I definitely feel shocked.

examples.note: Mari was physically and emotionally devastated by Haruki's betrayal; Todokanai TL assigns that damage to Haruki.
examples.japanese:
飼い犬に手を噛まれるなんてレベルじゃない、
とんでもない裏切りで、肉体的にも精神的にも
ボロボロにされたんだから。
examples.todokanai: It's not the pain of being bitten by a domestic dog; it's a tremendous betrayal piercing countless holes into my physical and mental being.

examples.note: Setsuna exposes herself by interpreting Haruki's vague reaction as assent; the English makes Haruki turn it into a definite statement.
examples.japanese:
俺の曖昧な反応を勝手に肯定と捉えたせいで、
馬脚を現してしまった。
examples.todokanai: As I turn my vague reaction into a definite statement, I reveal its true meaning.

examples.note: Haruki wants Setsuna to color him so completely that nobody else can move his heart; the English reverses the direction and has him stain her.
examples.japanese:
雪菜に、染められたい。
もう、俺が誰にも心を動かされることのないくらいに。
examples.todokanai: I want to… stain her with my color. To the point where no one else would ever make my heart race again.

examples.note: Setsuna pleads with Haruki not to hang up; the English changes who controls the threatened action and has Setsuna promise not to hang up.
examples.japanese:
「信じられない…
絶対に、絶対に…切っちゃ嫌ぁ」
examples.todokanai: "I don't believe you… I absolutely… absolutely… won't hang up!"

examples.note: Haruki asks Kazusa to check the article directly; the English says Haruki himself wants to perform the check.
examples.japanese:
「実は記事の最終チェック、
事務所通してると時間かかるから、
直接やってもらいたくてさ…」
examples.todokanai: "The truth is, the final checking of the articles will take a while if I do it at the office, so I wanted to do it directly…"

examples.note: Haruki condemns himself as Kazusa's accomplice in maintaining her facade; the English makes Kazusa shoulder his burden and calls her selfish.
examples.japanese: あいつの片棒を担いでる俺に。
examples.todokanai: She just selfishly shouldered what was supposed to be mine to bear.

examples.note: The adjacent turn and plural comparison support the subject supplied in English: Haruki and Setsuna are far behind the professional performers.
examples.japanese:
「服も、腕も、意気込みも…
どれも遠く及ばない」
examples.todokanai: "Their clothing, their skill, and even their enthusiasm… We're far behind them in just about every way."

examples.note: Todokanai TL preserves the shared subject and shared culpability: both Haruki and Kazusa knew the act was despicable, and neither stopped.
examples.japanese:
だって、五年前の俺たちも…
互いに『最悪のこと』ってわかってて、
それでも止まらなかっただけ、なんだから。
examples.todokanai: Because even five years ago… we both knew we were doing something despicable. We merely didn't stop in spite of that.

dossiers.title: Negation, polarity, and speech-act force
dossiers.claim: Todokanai TL sometimes keeps a scene's broad topic while reversing yes/no force or changing what a speaker is doing with a sentence. A prohibition becomes permission or impossibility, a question becomes an answer, a promise becomes a wish, and an obligation the speaker accepts becomes a demand imposed on someone else.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The force of compact Japanese dialogue depends on negative predicates, particles, imperative forms, rhetorical framing, and the preceding turn. English may restructure these forms, but it must preserve whether the line asks, forbids, promises, concedes, challenges, or assigns an obligation.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: These changes recast relationships. Haruki's promise to respect Mari's boundaries becomes concern for whether she likes him; his duty to confess becomes Setsuna's duty to listen; Takeya's flirtatious joke becomes a request to be excluded; and a sexual prohibition becomes an announcement that movement will begin. The surviving subject matter conceals a reversed interpersonal act.
dossiers.limits: Negative questions and elliptical commands cannot be translated word for word, and a natural English answer may invert surface polarity while preserving meaning. These findings require the operative proposition or speech act to change. The counterexamples show a prohibition and a negative reassurance whose force survives idiomatic restructuring.

examples.note: Mari concludes she can only be one of two alternatives; the English says she is neither, reversing her conclusion.
examples.japanese: （その、どっちかでしか、ないんだな…）
examples.todokanai: (I'm neither of those things in the end, huh…)

「ああ約束する。
もう学園祭まではギターのことしか考えない。
その代わり、信じさせてもらうからな」
examples.todokanai: "Yeah, I promise. I won't think about anything else but the guitar until the school festival. But in return, I want you to promise me something."

examples.note: Setsuna challenges the rule that one must not love a terrible person; the English changes moral prohibition into factual impossibility.
examples.japanese:
「最低な人を好きになっちゃいけないなんて、
一体誰が決めたのよ！？」
examples.todokanai: "Who ever decided that it's impossible to like horrible people?"

examples.note: Haruki tells Setsuna not to move during sex; the English reverses it into announcing that he will start moving.
examples.japanese: 「だから、動く…な」
examples.todokanai: "So I'll begin moving now… okay?"

examples.note: Takeya asks when Haruki is available; the English instead grants Haruki open-ended availability.
examples.japanese:
「いつならＯＫなんだよ？
もうすぐ３月だぞ？」
examples.todokanai: "Whenever you'd like is okay, got it? And it's almost March, you know?"

examples.note: Takeya jokes that if the women fight it should at least be over him; the English says to leave him out of it.
examples.japanese:
「お前らなぁ…
修羅場るならせめて俺を巡ってにしてくれよ」
examples.todokanai: "Listen, you two… Please leave me out of it if you're going to come to blows."

「…あの時はごめんなさい。
俺、もう、麻理さんの嫌がることはしないから」
examples.todokanai: "…I'm really sorry for what happened back then. It's just that I don't want you to hate me anymore, Mari-san."

examples.japanese:
「話があるんだ。
どうしても言わなくちゃならない、大事な…」
examples.todokanai: "I have something to tell you. It's something important, something you absolutely have to hear…"

examples.note: Haruki's rhetorical 'Then why? That's the question' becomes an answer to a question Setsuna never asked.
examples.japanese:
「だったら何で？　というわけだ。
わかった？　秘密兵器のボーカルさん？」
examples.todokanai: "That's my answer to you asking why. Got it, Miss Secret-weapon-singer?"

examples.note: Haruki asks how often Takeya and Io must confirm his answer; the English makes them repeatedly tell him the answer.
examples.japanese:
「さっきから何度確かめれば気が済むんだよ…
行く予定なんかないって言ってるだろ」
examples.todokanai: "How many times do you have to tell me that…? I've already told you I have no intention of going."

examples.note: The English naturally restructures Kazusa's compressed self-prohibition while preserving both claims: this is wrong, and Haruki belongs to Setsuna.
examples.japanese:
「駄目だって…間違えるな…
こいつは雪菜のものなんだから…」
examples.todokanai: "I can't… This is a mistake… He belongs to Setsuna…"

examples.note: Io's negative reassurance is handled correctly: Haruki is not in the wrong, and Io was happy because she had witnessed Setsuna's tears.

「ううん、悪くない。
むしろあたしだって、とっても嬉しかった。
…ずっと雪菜の側で、あの子の涙、見てきたからね」
