examples.todokanai: The white semen that shot out of my penis slowly oozed down onto the bed in a thick trickle.

examples.note: Haruki describes extracting Koharu's saliva and using his own tongue to carry it to the back of his throat. The English instead guides Koharu's tongue itself to the back of his throat, inventing a substantially different physical action in an otherwise explicit, sequential description.
examples.japanese:
その熱い口中を蹂躙したり、
本能のままに小春の唾液を搾り取って、
自分の喉の奥まで舌を伝って運び込んだりしない。
examples.todokanai: I wouldn't be imposing myself upon her warm mouth and guiding her tongue to the back of my throat as if on instinct to indulge in her saliva like this.

examples.note: After Koharu urges him to undress too, Haruki tears open his own buttons and throws off his own outerwear. The translation assigns both garments and actions to Koharu, changing who is being undressed.
examples.japanese:
小春に言われるまでもなく、
引きちぎるようにボタンを外し、
上着を脱ぎ捨てていく。
examples.todokanai: Before Koharu could say anything, I'd already torn off the last of her buttons and tossed her blazer aside.

examples.note: The semen is visibly on Izumi's abdomen after explicit withdrawal and external ejaculation. The English puts it inside her, reversing the location and contradicting the approved source note's limit on what the scene establishes.
examples.japanese:
だから、和泉が自分のお腹にかかった白濁を手に取り、
ゆっくりと目の前に透かしてみたりした時には…
examples.todokanai: Since Izumi takes the clouded substance that had become trapped inside her with her own hands and carefully raises it to examine it…

examples.note: Mari is being penetrated by Haruki, letting out intense gasps, and appealing to him with a painfully yearning expression. The English turns the penetration into her sobs metaphorically piercing his heart and changes gasps to sobs, replacing the sentence's explicit physical agent and action.
examples.japanese:
俺に貫かれ、激しい喘ぎ声を漏らしながら、
すごく切なそうな表情で、俺に訴えかける。
examples.todokanai: She cries with an incredibly heartrending expression, and her sobs pierce my heart.

examples.note: Kazusa says she was first to kiss him, embrace him, and fall in love with him. 抱きあった is mutual embracing, not sex; 'making love' invents an impossible sexual encounter while Haruki was asleep and corrupts the revelation's exact hierarchy of firsts.
examples.japanese:
「キスしたのも、抱きあったのも。
…そいつのこと好きになったのも」
examples.todokanai: "Kissing him, making love to him… and falling in love with him."

examples.note: Haruki says that if he embraces Kazusa, he will never be able to let her go again. Although the surrounding proposal is sexual, 抱きしめる here is deliberately the emotional act of holding her; the English turns it into intercourse and destroys the hold/let-go parallel.
examples.japanese:
「愛してるって言ったら、
お前が世界で一番になっちまう！
抱きしめたら、二度と離せなくなる！」
examples.todokanai: "If I say that I love you, you'll become the most precious person in the world to me! If I make love to you, I won't ever be able to let you go!"

examples.note: Kazusa says it is coming into a place different from usual—her anus rather than her vagina. The English makes Kazusa the agent who put it somewhere, reversing the action in her immediate bodily report after Haruki ejaculates inside her.
examples.japanese:
「はぁ、あ、あぁぁ…あんっ、んっ、んぅぅ…
うあぁぁ…いつもと違うとこ、入ってきて…ぅぇぇ…」
examples.todokanai: "Aah, ah, aaah. Ahn, mh, mhh… Uaaah… I put it inside somewhere… different from usual… aaah…"

examples.note: Io continues by asking whether the rumor that Takeya loses interest after sleeping with a woman once was true. Todokanai TL omits the sexual accusation that triggers his demand for her source and leaves the quotation open.
examples.japanese:
「お前、中学の時からずっとあたし狙ってたくせに！
一度寝たら興味失うって本当だったのかよ！？」
examples.todokanai: "That's rich, considering you've been trying to get with me since middle school!

examples.note: Kazusa's declaration that she will embrace and kiss Haruki and continue until they go all the way remains explicit in English; neither the escalation nor her initiative is sanitized.
examples.japanese:
「あたし、お前を思いっきり抱きしめるぞ？
ものすごい勢いでキスするぞ？
最後まで止まらないぞ？」
examples.todokanai: "I'll hug you with all my heart. I'll kiss you with such fervor that I won't be able to stop until we've gone all the way, you know."

examples.note: The English preserves the mutual continuation of the scene: from this point both partners proceed and neither stops before the end. It does not assign the action or resolve to only one participant.
examples.japanese:
そこから先は、
もう二人とも、最後まで止まらない。
examples.todokanai: Now that we've come this far, the two of us won't stop until the very end.

dossiers.title: Idioms, metaphors, and literalization
dossiers.claim: Across unrelated chapters and speakers, Todokanai TL repeatedly maps a conspicuous component of a Japanese idiom onto an English word or stock phrase without preserving the idiom's proposition. The problem is not literalness by itself: it is that the resulting English describes a different action, assigns a different character judgment, or becomes impossible to parse.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The scripts use both fixed idioms and scene-specific figurative systems. Their operative meaning is normally established by the surrounding reply, physical action, or later repetition: a back 'speaks,' a guilty belly can be probed, emotional distance is measured as temperature, and a familiar locution can describe indifference without naming wind at all.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The recurring surface-first reading produces cemetery decoration, misplaced embarrassment, an invented female employee, an accusation of duplicity inside a compliment, literal body heat during a relational argument, and phrases such as 'concealed shadows' that are not English propositions. Because several figures recur, a local error can also break a route-wide metaphor rather than merely one sentence.
dossiers.limits: Literal translation is not inherently defective, and domesticating an idiom is often the strongest solution. A finding is included only where the English proposition or active image changes materially. The counterexamples show both a natural English-proverb substitution and a culturally adapted workplace idiom that preserve function without copying Japanese wording.

examples.note: Fujishiro jokes that from beyond the grave he will at least wave a white flag of surrender. The translation instead puts the flag on Takeya's grave, reversing both whose grave is imagined and what happens to the flag.
examples.japanese:
「頑張ってくれ飯塚。成功を祈ってるぞ。
草葉の陰から白旗くらいは振っててやるからな」
examples.todokanai: "Hang in there, Iizuka. I'll be praying for your success. And I'll be sure to put a white flag on your grave!"

examples.note: Takeya means “and you're lecturing me even as you say that.” “Speak of the devil” is the wrong English idiom: nobody has just appeared after being mentioned.
examples.japanese: 「言ってる側から説教だし」
examples.todokanai: "Speak of the devil, here it comes again…"

examples.note: With the festival entry filed and the program nearly at press, Takeya says they must get a viable performance together at any cost. 'Pull ourselves together' may suggest rallying, but it loses the concrete production outcome carried by 形にする.
examples.japanese:
「もうエントリーは済んでるし、
プログラムも入稿寸前だし、
…何が何でも形にしないと」
examples.todokanai: "We've already signed up to perform at the festival, and the program has to be submitted shortly… We have to pull ourselves together somehow."

examples.note: 頭が上がらない means Haruki is even more indebted to, outmatched by, or unable to take a superior position toward Setsuna after her recovery. The English reads the image literally as difficulty making eye contact and changes the relationship judgment into embarrassment.
examples.japanese:
とにかくこれで、
今まで以上に雪菜に頭が上がらなくなってしまった。
examples.todokanai: After this, I'm sure that I'll have even more trouble looking her in the eyes…

examples.note: 陰ひなたなく/陰ひなたから支える means supporting someone both publicly and behind the scenes. Todokanai TL reads the light-and-shadow idiom as duplicity, making Setsuna call dependable Haruki two-faced in the middle of praising him.
examples.japanese:
「普段と同様、いつもわたしたちメンバーを、
陰ひなたから支えてくれる、
とても頼りがいのある人です」
examples.todokanai: "And just as he's done for many of you, he was the one driving us on and supporting us through his two-faced nature. He's someone that we could always depend on."

examples.note: The idiom means the accusation is not exactly right but is not far off. The literalized English instead discusses physical distance and obscures the proposition.
examples.japanese:
「ま、当たらずとも遠からずなんじゃない？
さ、大通りまで出るわよ」
examples.todokanai: "Well, it's not too close or too far, right? Come on, let's walk to the main street."

examples.note: 何処吹く風 means acting as though another person's agitation is no concern of yours. Mari slowly stands as if Haruki's panic means nothing to her. The English decomposes the idiom into an incoherent literal gust of air that she somehow 'bequeaths' him.
examples.japanese:
そんな、俺の焦燥なんか何処吹く風みたいに、
麻理さんがゆっくり立ち上がる。
examples.todokanai: Mari-san slowly stood up, as if to blow a gust of fresh air to bequeath my flustered self.

examples.note: 女手一つで means Youko raised her daughter single-handedly as a woman or single mother. The translation invents a separate female employee who helped her raise Kazusa.
examples.japanese:
「当たり前だ。
そうやって女手一つでこんなワガママ娘を育てたんだ。
どこに嫌われる理由があるんだよ」
examples.todokanai: "Of course not. She raised such a spoiled daughter with the help of a single female worker. Why would you ever hate her?"

examples.note: Kazusa says Haruki's criticism hits painfully close to home because it also describes them. The translation treats it as merely a rough situation and loses the line's rebound onto their affair.
examples.japanese: 「それは…耳が痛いな」
examples.todokanai: "That sounds rough…"

examples.note: Haruki fears they will probe a belly that is not entirely pain-free: unlike the idiom's innocent person, he really does have secrets to uncover. The translation reduces this guilt-laden risk to a generic bad time.
examples.japanese:
今日の浮かれた日に、この人たちに付き合ってると、
痛くも無くない腹を探られるかもしれないから
さっさと職場から逃げ出した。
examples.todokanai: If I spend any more time with these people on a day as festive as today, I feel like I'm going to have a bad time, so I run away from my post.

examples.note: Haruki senses the figurative temperature gap widening between his feverish fantasy of future seasons together and Kazusa's cooling, lonely response. The English makes it a difference in their literal body temperatures, breaking the scene's emotional thermometer.
examples.japanese:
けれど俺は、徐々に広がる温度差を感じていながらも、
そこで言葉を切る器用さを持ち合わせていなかった。
examples.todokanai: But no matter how big the difference in our body temperatures becomes, I can't stop myself from speaking.

examples.note: Haruki has tried to remain deliberately insensitive to the widening figurative temperature gap between his desperate insistence and Kazusa's resolve to send him back. The English again literalizes emotional temperature as body heat, despite no bodily-temperature contrast in this train argument.
examples.japanese: かずさとの温度差に、鈍感でいようとしてた。
examples.todokanai: I tried to ignore the difference in body temperature between us.

examples.note: Setsuna accuses Takahiro of constantly seizing on verbal slips and inconsistencies. 'Grasp at straws' means making a desperate weak attempt, not pedantically catching somebody's wording, so the English accusation is the wrong one.
examples.japanese: 「っ！　どうしてそういう揚げ足ばっかり取るのよ！」
examples.todokanai: "…! Why do you have to grasp at straws like that!?"

examples.note: 影を潜める means both women's characteristic forms of chatter remained absent. The literalized 'concealed shadows' leaves the governing proposition unintelligible.
examples.japanese:
「それじゃ、そろそろ…」

「うん…」

　部屋の時計は、十時二十分…別れの時は、いつもより十分も早く訪れた。

　結局、最後まで二人の会話が盛り返すことはなかった。

　ころころと話題が変わる雪菜の気ままなお喋りも、言葉と口調が乖離しっぱなしの、かずさの愛情だだ漏れの悪口も、影を潜めたままだった。

「…おやすみ」

「っ、あ、待ってかずさ！」

「ん？」
examples.todokanai:
“Then, I guess it’s about time for me to…”

“Yeah…”

The clock in her room read 10:20… Their parting time had come ten minutes earlier than usual.

In the end, their conversation never made a comeback.

Setsuna’s freewheeling chitchat, changing topics at the drop of a hat, and Kazusa’s badmouthing that was bursting with affection, her words and tone perpetually divergent from each other, both concealed shadows.

“…Good night.”

“…Ah, wait, Kazusa!”

“Hm?”

examples.note: A Japanese preparation proverb is replaced by a natural English proverb. Its warning function survives, and Kazusa's following response still has a coherent target; this is successful domestication rather than formal imitation.
examples.japanese:
「備えあれば憂いなし。
俺もたまにはいいこと言うだろ？」
examples.todokanai: "By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail. I say some pretty cool things sometimes, huh?"

examples.note: Localizing the exploitative-workplace label ブラック as 'sweatshop' preserves the publishing-industry joke and lets the speakers escalate it naturally. The substitution demonstrates that cultural adaptation can be both free and faithful.
examples.japanese:
「ホント期待してるからね小春っち。何しろ最近のウチ、その“ただのアルバイト”が一週間続いたことないんだよねぇ」

「そういうこと言うのやめてよ鈴木さん。それだとウチがまるでブラックみたいじゃん」

「何言ってんだ松岡、ブラックでない出版社が生き残ってる訳ないだろこの出版不況のご時世に」

「木崎さんもさらっと肯定しちゃったらマズいでしょ……」

　しかしまぁ、ここにいる人たちは、社会の先輩として人間ができているのか、それとも心底いい加減なのか、彼女の堅苦しい態度をさらっと受け流して勝手に盛り上がる。
examples.todokanai:
“We’ve got high hopes for you, Kohacchi. Lately, none of our part-timers have stuck around for more than a week…”

“Don’t say stuff like that, Suzuki-san. You’ll make us sound like a sweatshop.”

“What are you talking about, Matsuoka? In times like these, with publications in such a slump, no publishing company could survive without being a sweatshop.”

“Do you have to affirm that so readily, Kizaki-san…?”

But, well, whether it was because they were more experienced members of society as her seniors, or whether they were all just completely irresponsible, the others present let her formal attitude wash right off of them and got swept up in their own lively conversations.

dossiers.title: Comic, rhetorical, and metalinguistic structure
dossiers.claim: A recurring class of Todokanai TL errors preserves the conversational topic but deletes the verbal hinge that makes the exchange work: a correction, repeated word, one-character contrast, malformed proverb, grammatical label, or deliberately misused term. The result is often fluent enough in isolation yet causally broken once the next reply is read.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Maruto frequently writes dialogue as a mechanism spanning several turns. One speaker changes a particle, mangles a proverb, answers a badly formed question with the wrong datum, or repeats an opponent's exact word; another speaker's response is the payoff and therefore evidence for what the first line must do.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: When the hinge is normalized into generic dialogue, the reply becomes an overreaction or non sequitur, character-specific verbal precision disappears, and recurring jokes collapse into bare plot information. The loss is rhetorical and structural even where the broad scene event remains understandable.
dossiers.limits: The dossier does not require reproducing Japanese phonemes, particles, or kanji contrasts mechanically. An English joke may use a different device if it motivates the same response and preserves the relational function. The counterexamples demonstrate successful coinage, comic compression, and direct preservation of a culturally legible punch line.

examples.note: Takeya grandly asks who could stop her passion and then literally says “rhetorical question,” reading out the grammatical device as part of his evasive joke. The translation invents a claim about her refusing to be stopped and deletes the joke.
examples.japanese:
「自分の奥底にある想いを精一杯表現したいって情熱を
誰が止めることができようか反語…」
examples.todokanai: "The burning passion deep inside of her was just dying to burst out, as if to say she wouldn't allow anyone to get in her way…"

examples.note: The joke pivots from 懐柔, “to win someone over,” to the literal 柔, “soft”: whatever Tomo used on Haruki looked very soft indeed. Calling “persuade” an understatement neither conveys the physical insinuation nor forms an English joke.
examples.japanese:
…まさに『懐柔』という言葉が
ぴったり来るくらいに柔らかそうだった。
examples.todokanai: …Yeah, the word "persuade" is definitely an understatement.

examples.note: Haruki claims he has merely been meaning to say this for a while; Takeya's next line punctures the pose by saying Haruki has told him clearly many times. The English has Haruki concede that at once, destroying the retort.
examples.japanese:
「前から言おうと思ってたんだけどな武也…
今日こそはハッキリ言わせてもらうぞ」
examples.todokanai: "I've told you this before, Takeya… so I'll spell it out clearly for you today."

examples.note: Chikashi has asked whether Haruki has an ate—a lead or prospect—and Haruki answers saa, “who knows,” changing a single sound. Chikashi explicitly protests that one-character substitution. The English retains only generic anxiety and erases the joke it is reacting to.
examples.japanese:
「さり気なく一文字すり替えるなよ！
思いっきり不安になるじゃないか！」
examples.todokanai: "Don't just casually say that! You're making me feel uneasy here!"

examples.note: Haruki has deliberately corrupted the fixed proverb 若いうちの苦労は買ってでもせよ, replacing youthful hardship with youthful stupidity, so that Takeya agrees before Haruki springs the correction. The English supplies an ordinary-sounding maxim instead of a visibly mangled proverb, leaving “No they don't” without the source joke's mechanism.
examples.japanese:
「それに…
『若いうちの馬鹿は買ってでもしろ』って言うだろ？」
examples.todokanai: "Besides, people say 'fool around while you're still young,' right?"

examples.note: Setsuna has changed the earlier 雪菜でいい, 'Setsuna is fine,' to 雪菜がいい, 'Setsuna is the one I want.' The narration explicitly calls the one-particle change a power-up, but the translation repeats the same instruction and emphasizes 'should,' so the grammatical escalation no longer exists.
examples.japanese: 『雪菜“が”いいからね』
examples.todokanai: "From now on, you 'should' call me Setsuna."

examples.note: Haruki says he is bad at English only relatively; Setsuna replies that she is bad at politics and economics absolutely. “I know that for a fact” removes the explicit relative/absolute pair on which their teasing exchange is built.
examples.japanese: 「わたしだって政治も経済も苦手だよ。絶対的に」
examples.todokanai: "Well, I'm bad at politics and economics too. I know that for a fact."

examples.note: Haruki tells Chiaki to revise or formulate her question properly before asking it, then deliberately answers with the time instead of the weekday. “Take a guess” neither translates that metalinguistic correction nor supports Chiaki's immediate response that she did not confuse her meaning, breaking the exchange's mechanism.
examples.japanese:
「人にものを尋ねるときはちゃんと推敲してからにしろ。
１１時だよ」
examples.todokanai: "You should at least try to take a guess before asking someone. It's 11 o'clock already."

examples.note: Haruki protests that Takeya's mangled “fish eyes” expression is awful; Takeya misreads him as complaining about the light tap and answers accordingly. “That hurt” makes Haruki explicitly complain about physical pain and removes the misunderstanding that motivates his grammatical correction.
examples.japanese:
「げほっ、げほぉっ…
た、武也…お前、酷いぞそれ」
examples.todokanai: "Kgh, agh… T-Takeya… That hurt, man."

examples.note: Haruki calls it 'a little cruel friendship,' an oxymoronic phrase whose 残酷 is explicitly picked up by the next line. The translation deletes cruelty, changes the proposition to ordinary teasing, and strands the reply's verbal callback.
examples.japanese:
「あっははは…意地になんないでよ春希。
ちょっとした残酷な友情じゃんか～」
examples.todokanai: "Ahahaha… No need to be like that, Haruki. Poking fun at each other is what friends do, isn't it?"

examples.note: Haruki corrects the phrase to 語るに落ちた, meaning that someone's own speech inadvertently reveals the truth. The English glosses it as being “done for,” failing precisely where the scene pauses to correct Satou's Japanese and then reuses the phrase.
examples.japanese: 「語るに落ちた、だ」
examples.todokanai: "You mean to say that I'm done for."

examples.note: After Setsuna mistakenly says low atmospheric pressure, Haruki deliberately refrains from correcting her to low blood pressure because of the mood. The translation invents medical reassurance and loses the pressure-word correction.
examples.japanese:
『低血圧だろ』という指摘は、
この場の空気を冷静に鑑みて敢えてスルーした。
examples.todokanai: I realized, after thinking about it for a moment, that "low blood pressure isn't something you should worry about" isn't an appropriate comment to make in this situation.

examples.note: The editor asks whether Mari is sane—正気. She replies that she had hoped he would ask whether she was serious—本気. Rendering both words as 'serious' erases the one-character contrast and the joke that he treats her decision as insanity rather than mere bluffing.
examples.japanese: 「メールの件、正気じゃないよな？」
examples.todokanai: "About the email you sent me, you weren't serious, now, were you?"

examples.note: Kazusa says the comparison makes her look like a 小者—a smaller figure or small fry beside Youko—and Haruki affectionately repeats 小者っぽい three lines later. The English first invents deficient natural skill and then calls her an upstart, so the repeated self-deprecating label no longer binds the exchange.
examples.japanese:
「そう書かれると、
母さんに比べてあたしが随分と小者に見えるな」
examples.todokanai: "If you write that, it'll look like I'm trying to make up for my lack of natural skill."

examples.note: Suzuki wonders how a famous beauty like Setsuna ever got caught by such a stiff, straitlaced man. Todokanai TL omits the insult and leaves the quote open, so Matsuoka's sexual answer that Haruki was probably 'stiff in various ways' loses the word it is punning on.
examples.japanese:
「ちょっと洒落になんないもんね～北原君の奥さん。
ナイツレコードの美人広報って業界でも有名なんだよね？
なんでこんな堅物に引っかかっちゃったかなぁ」
examples.todokanai: "Your wife is something else, isn't she? She's famous in the industry as the public relations beauty of Knights Records.

examples.note: The coined nickname 小春希 fuses Koharu with Haruki while belittling her as his smaller copy. 'Mini-Haruki' is compact, immediately intelligible, and recreates the obnoxious English nickname function without a translator's note.
examples.japanese: 「小春希」
examples.todokanai: "Mini-Haruki."

examples.note: The English keeps the extended joke that Io and Takeya's rotten bond has decomposed over six years and vanished without a trace. It compresses naturally without discarding the image or punch line.
examples.japanese:
「六年経つと、
腐った後に分解されて、跡形もなくなるけどね」
examples.todokanai: "That bond's as good as rotten and gone without a trace after these six years, though."

examples.note: The direct 'Please save me, Helen Keller' preserves the triple-affliction setup and remains immediately legible as the punch line. No explanatory padding is required for the joke to work.
examples.japanese: 助けてヘレンケラー…
examples.todokanai: Please save me, Helen Keller…

dossiers.title: Literary allusion and cultural reference
dossiers.claim: Across these passages, Todokanai TL repeatedly preserves an immediate plot proposition while deleting, misassigning, or substituting the literary mechanism that gives it force. Several references demonstrably recur—the Spider's Thread, the Heavenly Rock Cave, the North Wind, paired proverbs, and theatrical roles—so their loss also weakens the script's observable system of rescue, refusal, exposure, appetite, and persuasion.
dossiers.sourcePattern: Named works and culturally familiar phrases supply miniature stories whose roles the local scene assigns to the cast. Miyazawa's language describes Haruki's impossible ideal and his predatory restaurant structures the ticket joke; Akutagawa's single thread repeatedly marks salvation that can snap; Amaterasu's cave marks Kazusa's seclusion; the North Wind and the Sun allocate traveler, force, and warm persuasion; paired Basho parodies and repeated theatrical or folkloric roles depend on recognizable wording and recall.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The English often leaves a superficially intelligible sentence while stripping the shared literary memory beneath it. A spider's thread becomes either a generic fine thread or an invented romantic tether; the Heavenly Rock Cave becomes an ordinary hiding place; Basho becomes miscellaneous banter; the North Wind fable changes who is traveler, wind, or sun; and canonical titles or roles become unexplained romanization or a different tale. Readers can follow events but lose the network by which later scenes reinterpret earlier ones.
dossiers.limits: An English translation need not retain Japanese phrasing, add translator's notes, or make every culturally familiar reference equally explicit. A reference counts as preserved when its operative image, role structure, joke, or named-work identity remains recoverable in natural English. The counterexamples show Todokanai TL doing exactly that with Helen Keller and Snow Country. The dossier does not treat ordinary idioms as literary allusions merely because they have cultural history.

examples.note: Kazusa's escalating parallel description culminates in an unmistakable adaptation of the cadence and wording of Miyazawa Kenji's Ame ni mo Makezu. The English conveys the component traits as ordinary explanatory prose but does not recreate or signal the literary echo that structures the characterization.
examples.japanese:
「非競争主義、脱落者ゼロ、一緒にゴール。
決して人とは争わず、いつも静かに笑ってる」
examples.todokanai: "You avoid competition, you make sure no one's left behind and that everyone makes it to the end together. You don't oppose anyone, always smiling quietly."

examples.note: Haruki explicitly invokes Miyazawa's The Restaurant of Many Orders: Takeya's tickets impose one condition after another until they figuratively devour him, as the restaurant intends to devour its guests. The English invents a restaurant billing scam and erases the named literary mechanism.
examples.japanese:
武也が売りつけた『映画のチケット』は、
まるで注文の多い料理店のように、
徐々に俺を食い物にしていった。
examples.todokanai: Takeya's movie ticket deal makes me feel like I was just in one of those restaurants that adds things to your bill without you being aware of it, gradually prying your money away.

examples.note: The source pointedly calls his last hope 蜘蛛の糸, “the spider's thread,” invoking Akutagawa's story and its single thread of salvation. “That fine thread” removes the title phrase and therefore the literary image that organizes Haruki's sudden reversal from failure to hope.
examples.japanese:
だけど、そのポカの果て。
最後の最後の最後に、
たった一つの蜘蛛の糸を掴み取った。
examples.todokanai: But, at the end of that blunder, right at the end of it all, I'd grabbed that fine thread.

examples.note: The image invokes Akutagawa's The Spider's Thread: the last slender means of salvation snaps just as Haruki's pretense is exposed. The source does not describe a thread binding Haruki's and Setsuna's hands together; that invented romantic tether misconstrues the allusion's rescue-and-fall logic.
examples.japanese:
…結局、俺の方はただの“フリ”だったってことがバレて、
手元からぷつんと蜘蛛の糸が切れてしまったことも。
examples.todokanai: …And I told her about how the spider's thread that bound our hands together snapped at the very moment I was caught in the act of being insincere.

examples.note: Haruki explicitly calls his fragile lead 蜘蛛の糸, invoking Akutagawa's The Spider's Thread before it snaps in his hands. The English replaces the named image with the generic phrase 'thread of hope,' erasing the literary allusion and its moral/desperate overtones.
examples.japanese:
結局、やっと掴んだと思った蜘蛛の糸は、
手元からあっさりと断ち切られてしまったから。
examples.todokanai: In the end, the moment I thought I'd finally gotten a hold of a thread of hope, it ended up snapping easily in my hands.

examples.note: This is a comic rewrite of the famous haiku 秋深き／隣は何を／する人ぞ: Haruki changes the wondering “What is my neighbor doing?” into “my neighbor does nothing.” The literal English leaves the allusion and the act of parody entirely invisible.
examples.japanese: 秋深し　隣はなにも　しない人
examples.todokanai: In the late autumn The neighboring student does Not a single thing

examples.note: This is the second parody of Basho's 秋深き／隣は何を／する人ぞ in the scene, so it should visibly recall the earlier altered haiku while splicing in the proverb 情けは人のためならず. The English neither preserves that paired literary callback nor has source support for the added phrase “Compassion's your call.”
examples.japanese: 秋深し　情けは人の　ためならず
examples.todokanai: In the late autumn What goes around comes around Compassion's your call

examples.note: The Amaterasu image is of the Heavenly Rock Door or barrier finally opening, with the opening itself as the grammatical subject. The English has Kazusa actively open a cave, muddying both the movement and the culturally recognizable image; the corresponding Coda reuse later loses it altogether.
examples.japanese:
その思いが通じたのかわからないけど…
とにかく、天の岩戸が、今やっと開いてくれた。
examples.todokanai: I have no idea how she interpreted my reply, but for now, I'm just glad she's finally opened the proverbial Heavenly Rock Cave.

examples.note: Haruki explicitly continues the Heavenly Rock Cave myth: he cannot imagine the world after Amaterasu emerges, so he cannot yet dance before the cave door to entice her out. The translation removes Amaterasu and replaces ritual dance with knocking, erasing the source's sustained mythic analogy.
examples.japanese:
だって俺はまだ、天照大神の出てきた後の世界を
自分の中にイメージできていない。
だから今、その扉の前で踊る訳には行かない。
examples.todokanai: Because I still don't know what will happen once she comes out to the world. That's why I can't knock on her door just yet.

examples.note: The image invokes the single traveler's coat from the North Wind fable, with Setsuna's storm unable to dislodge Haruki's decision. Plural passers-by turns the specific fable structure into a generic street scene.
examples.japanese:
旅人のコートも。
そして、俺の決断も。
examples.todokanai: Not the coats of passers-by, nor my determination.

examples.note: The line invokes 'The North Wind and the Sun': Setsuna is the traveler resisting the north wind, immovable by half-hearted force. Todokanai TL makes Haruki the traveler and turns the domestic persuasion problem into his own march against weather, breaking both agency and the fable setup.
examples.japanese:
こうなったときの彼女は、まさに北風に抗う旅人。
生半可な強制じゃ、てこでも動かない。
examples.todokanai: When she's like this, I feel like a lone traveler marching against the north wind. Ordinary means simply will not work.

examples.note: Continuing the fable, Haruki decides to bathe the resistant traveler Setsuna in sunlight—use warmth and temptation where force fails. Todokanai TL says the sun stops the north wind, which is not what happens in the fable and compounds the preceding reassignment of traveler and wind.
examples.japanese: そう、太陽の光を浴びせるまでだ。
examples.todokanai: Of course, the only thing capable of stopping the north wind is the sun.

examples.note: Calling Takahiro the household's grasshopper invokes The Ant and the Grasshopper and his failure to prepare; 'lackadaisical younger brother' deletes the fable image and its joke.
examples.japanese:
『そんなわけで、ウチのキリギリスな弟に、
何か言ってあげてください。
できればいつもの説教がいいな』
examples.todokanai: "That's why you should give some suggestions to my lackadaisical younger brother. It'd be great if you could lecture him, as usual."

examples.note: Tsuu is the singular crane-wife role Chiaki played in Junji Kinoshita's The Twilight Crane. Todokanai TL partially preserves the reference as the opaque romanization 'Yuutsuru,' but turns her one famous role into the plural characters of the play and therefore misstates the comparison with her Four Kashiwagi Sisters performance.
examples.japanese:
「中学の大会で演じた“つう”や、
付属祭で演じた“柏木四姉妹”と同じ、
一つの役なんだ」
examples.todokanai: "Much like how I single-handedly played the roles of the characters in Yuutsuru I performed in the middle school competition and The Four Kashiwagi Sisters during the high school festival."

examples.note: The Patrasche and freezing-to-death setup invokes the ending of A Dog of Flanders, and the narration completes it by saying Kazusa sleeps as though long since called to God. 'God-given elegance' replaces death with grace and breaks the allusive punch line.
examples.japanese:
いつもより人の少な目な学食には、一つのテーブルをまるまる占拠して試験後の解放感をかみしめる四人組の姿があった。

　春希と、その〝自称〟親友である飯塚武也と、その〝名実ともに〟悪友の水沢依緒と、そして…

「…すぅぅぅ」

「…そろそろ起きなよパトラッシュ。凍死するよ？」

「んぅ…？」

　今にも力尽きんと目をしょぼしょぼさせている春希の傍らで、とっくに神に召された趣で爆睡をかましているかずさと。

「冬馬さん、あんたさ、最近気を抜き過ぎじゃない？　色んな意味で」

「春希、お前さ、学園祭の時に九割の男を敵に回したけど、残り一割にまで喧嘩をふっかけるアグレッシブな男だったんだな…」
examples.todokanai:
In the cafeteria, which was less populated than usual, four people took up one table, digesting their sense of freedom in the aftermath of their exams.

Haruki, his self-proclaimed best friend Takeya Iizuka, his partner-in-crime, both in name and nature, Io Mizusawa, and…

“…Zzzz…”

“…Hey, Patrasche. Wake up before you freeze to death.”

“Hnn…?”

Next to Haruki, who was fighting with every ounce of his strength to keep his bleary eyes open, there was Kazusa, who had long since crashed out with all of her god-given elegance.

“Touma-san, haven’t you been a little too relaxed lately? In a few different senses.”

“Haruki, you already managed to make enemies of ninety percent of the guys here back during the school festival, and yet you’re aggressive enough to pick a fight with the last ten percent…”

examples.note: 三限寝太郎 is a high-confidence parody of 三年寝太郎, the folkloric 'Three-Year Sleeper,' replacing 'year' with the university term for class period after Haruki sleeps through three classes. The translation conveys the bare event but deletes the recreatable allusive nickname.
examples.japanese:
「起きろ！
この三限寝太郎！」
examples.todokanai: "Wake up! You slept through all three periods!"

examples.note: The Helen Keller name and the surrounding triple-affliction setup remain recognizable, so the reference continues to deliver its comic plea without explanatory debris.
examples.japanese: 助けてヘレンケラー…
examples.todokanai: Please save me, Helen Keller…

examples.note: Todokanai TL explicitly retains Snow Country and Kawabata in the tunnel-to-snow sequence. The capitalization is editorially loose, but the named work and the scene's operative comparison remain recoverable.
examples.japanese:
そこは、康成の言う『雪国』とは、
正確には違う場所ではあったけど…
examples.todokanai: The landscape we were greeted with was certainly a different place from the "Snow country" Yasunari wrote about…

dossiers.title: School, university, and institutional identity
dossiers.claim: Across all four sections, Todokanai TL repeatedly changes named faculties, school types, educational stages, and institutional relationships. These are not merely alternative labels for Japanese bureaucracy: the resulting English often identifies a different field, institution, qualification, age, or point in a student's career.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The source maintains a stable institutional map: Houjou University and its affiliated high school; the faculties of Political Science and Economics, Commerce, and Letters; private and national institutions; student teaching; junior college; advancement to higher education; and year levels stated relative to enrollment or graduation. These facts explain campus geography, finances, careers, and character timelines.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: Political Science and Economics becomes Public Policy, Commerce becomes Economics, a private high school becomes a prospective private university, student teaching becomes substitute employment, and university or high-school year markers move characters to different ages and stages. The cumulative English setting is recognizable but no longer administratively coherent.
dossiers.limits: English institutional labels may be naturalized and need not imitate Japanese ministry terminology. A finding requires the field, institution, school level, employment stage, or educational decision itself to change. The counterexamples show Todokanai TL successfully preserving both the music program's institutional history and the distinct school landmarks that connect present action to the trio's past.

examples.note: 商学部 is the faculty or department of commerce/business, not economics. The line gives Shouko's fabricated academic affiliation as a concrete identifying fact.
examples.japanese:
「長瀬晶子。商学部三年。
初めまして、小木曽雪菜さん」
examples.todokanai: "I'm Nagase Shouko. Economics Department, third year. Nice to meet you, Ogiso Setsuna-san."

examples.note: The café is the territory of the Political Science and Economics department, as the script itself spells out at the preceding location description. The English changes that department to Public Policy, creating an institutional and spatial inconsistency at the moment Haruki crosses into Setsuna's part of campus.
examples.japanese:
ここは、俺たち『文学部』の人間がいる場所じゃないのに。
彼女たち『政経』のテリトリーで。
examples.todokanai: This is no place for us "Literature" students. It's the "Public Policy" students' territory.

examples.note: Koharu says Mihoko has good grades and that their high school is private, so the school may have some administrative latitude about her attendance and graduation. The English instead says Mihoko is aiming for a private university, which provides no reason for the high school to accommodate her and misidentifies the relevant institution.
examples.japanese:
「あ、いえ、多分そんなことは…
美穂子、成績いいし、それに私立だから、
少しくらいは融通利くと思うし」
examples.todokanai: "Ah, no, I don't think that will be the case… Mihoko has good grades and she's aiming for a private university, after all, so I imagine there'll be room to accommodate her."

examples.note: 進学しない means Mihoko says she will not advance to higher education. The translation turns that future educational decision into refusal to attend school, changing the unresolved problem being discussed.
examples.japanese:
「その、解決できてない問題…
美穂子が進学しないって言い出した理由について、です」
examples.todokanai: "Um, about that problem that couldn't be solved…? I want to tell you the reason why Mihoko refused to go to school."

examples.note: 教育実習 is student teaching or a teaching practicum. Haruki is discussing returning as a trainee teacher, not being hired as a substitute teacher.
examples.japanese:
「じゃあ、今日は一体何の用なんです？
わたしのクラスに『偶然』教育実習にでも来ましたか？」
examples.todokanai: "So, what business do you have with me today? Did you just coincidentally get hired as our substitute teacher or something?"

examples.note: Tomo attends a junior college; the English calls it a vocational school.
examples.japanese:
「でも渚ってこっちの短大進んだよね？
早坂とは切れちゃったのかなぁ…
その辺りのこと、なんか言ってた？」
examples.todokanai: "But Nagisa got into a vocational school here, right? I wonder if she broke up with Hayasaka… At that time, did he say anything?"

examples.note: Uehara saw Chiaki's play at the affiliated high school's festival while he himself was a fourth-year university student. The English places his 'fourth year' in high school, producing a nonexistent school year and blurring the joke that he is now a seventh-year university student.
examples.japanese:
「例の付属祭でやった『雨月山の鬼』…
四年の時あれ見て思いっきり引き込まれてね。
彼女が大学に進学してくれたときは歓喜したよ」
examples.todokanai: "I was deeply fascinated when I watched The Demon of Mt. Uzuki being performed in high school back when I was in my fourth year. I must admit I was really delighted when I heard she was enrolling at this university."

examples.note: Haruki asks whether Takahiro is aiming for a national university, contrasted with a university outside the region. The translation changes the public institutional category into a prestige ranking.
examples.japanese:
『どこ受けるって？　国立狙い？
それとも地方の大学とか？』
examples.todokanai: "What university does he want to be accepted to? One of the top universities? Or perhaps a local one?"

examples.note: 大卒二年目 means someone in the second year after graduating from university. Haruki is a second-year member of the workforce, not a graduate student.
examples.japanese: 「大卒二年目を二年生って言うんならな…」
examples.todokanai: "I guess if you count a second-year grad student as a 'second-year'…"

examples.note: This is Setsuna's second year of high school, not second grade. In English, 'second grade' places the famous school idol in elementary school and makes the ensuing Miss Houjou High history temporally absurd.
examples.japanese:
「だって２年の頃の雪菜って、評判の学園アイドルじゃん。
俺と接点ができるなんて夢にも思わないって」
examples.todokanai: "But in second grade you were the famous school idol, Setsuna. I never even imagined I'd ever get a chance to talk to you."

examples.note: Haruki says he currently intends to enter political science and economics, the 政経 course or faculty. “Public policy” is a different academic field and breaks the department comparison Setsuna immediately begins.
examples.japanese: 「え？　いや、今のところ政経のつもりだけど…」
examples.todokanai: "Eh? No, right now I'm thinking along the lines of public policy…"

examples.note: The English keeps University High, its classroom and gymnasium, and Music Room 2 distinct as Haruki searches locations shared by the recent and five-year-old timelines.
examples.japanese:
真っ先に、閉門前の峰城大付属に駆け込み、
教室、体育館、第二音楽室…
そんな数日前と数年前の共通項は、見事に空振った。
examples.todokanai: First I went to Houjou High before closing, checked the classrooms, gymnasium, and Music Room 2. …She had been to those places both a few days ago and many years ago, but she was nowhere to be found.

examples.note: The English accurately preserves University High's prestigious music program, its history of producing professional performers, and the exceptional status of Kazusa's award within that history.
examples.japanese:
もともと、多数のプロを輩出している
峰城大付属音楽科ではあったけど、その中でも久々の
スマッシュヒットと言える今回の受賞だったらしい。
examples.todokanai: Even for the prestigious music program of Houjou High, which has produced many successful alumni, this award could still be considered an extraordinary accomplishment.

dossiers.title: Place names, transit, and spatial relations
dossiers.claim: Repeated lines replace named places with generic descriptions, truncate confirmed names, reverse arrivals and departures, or alter the physical relation between stations, roads, buildings, and destinations. The errors damage both immediate staging and the route-wide geography through which the story revisits its past.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The scripts use recurring stations and districts—Minami-Suetsugu, Suetsugucho, Arumi, Onjuku—as narrative coordinates. They also carefully track whether a train is arriving or departing, whether a location lies behind or inside a station, how far one landmark is from another, and which city or station a traveler has reached.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: Arumi becomes merely a place near the sea; Suetsugucho loses part of its name; an underpass becomes a security guard; an arriving train departs; a character already at a station is still traveling toward it; and Paris, Strasbourg, and nearby apartments are spatially reassigned. Readers can follow the broad journey while losing the exact map and timing.
dossiers.limits: Romanization choice alone is not treated as a material error, and English may reorganize a route description for fluency. Findings require a name to disappear or be truncated, or a physical/transit proposition to change. The counterexamples show Todokanai TL preserving Arumi and the relative geography of Suetsugucho, Minami-Suetsugu, the school, and Setsuna's home.

examples.note: Dinner in the proper-name location Arumi becomes dinner 'near the sea.'
examples.japanese:
「それに有海で夕食だと帰り遅くなるし、
何言ってんだろうな、俺」
examples.todokanai: "Besides, after having dinner near the sea, it'll be very late, so what am I even saying…"

examples.note: Haruki rides one station past his usual stop, Minami-Suetsugu, gets off at Suetsugucho, then walks fifteen minutes. The translation makes travel between the two stations his usual route and loses the meaningful act of passing his normal stop.
examples.japanese:
いつもの南末次から一駅乗り越して、
末次町で降りてそこから徒歩１５分。
examples.todokanai: It would usually take me a station's travel from Minami-Suetsugu to Suetsugu-chou, after which I'd need to take a fifteen-minute walk.

examples.note: The station is Suetsugucho Station, matching the established place name 末次町. Todokanai TL drops the -cho element from the station name.
examples.japanese:
ヒールで道路を蹴飛ばすと、がりっという嫌な音が意外に大きく響き、ヒールと雪菜の寿命をちょっとだけ縮める。

　末次町駅から家までの徒歩十五分の道のりを、雪菜はさっきからそんなふうに時には毒づきつつ、時には落ち込みつつ、時には興奮しつつ早足で歩く。
examples.todokanai:
As Setsuna pushed off the street with her heel hard, she heard an unexpectedly loud, unpleasant cracking sound, shortening the lifespan of both Setsuna and the heel by a bit.

She took the fifteen-minute walk from Suetsugu Station to her house quickly, sometimes cursing like that, sometimes falling into depression, sometimes getting agitated.

examples.note: ガード is the railway underpass they pass beneath on the way to the familiar apartment. The translation invents a security guard and corrupts the route description.
examples.japanese:
ガードをくぐった先の、
見慣れたマンションが、ある。
examples.todokanai: After passing the guard, we see a familiar apartment building.

examples.note: The announcement says the Onjuku-bound train will arrive shortly. Todokanai TL says it is about to depart, reversing the train's movement before the later announcement that it actually leaves without Setsuna.
examples.japanese:
「まもなく、一番線御宿行きが参ります。
白線の内側までお下がりください」
examples.todokanai: "The train on Line 1 toward Onjuku will depart shortly. Please stay within the white lines."

examples.note: Kazusa says she herself has just arrived at the station. The translation says she is still traveling toward it, contradicting her physical presence there.
examples.japanese:
「なんてな…ははっ、信じたか？
本当は、金曜からまだ一度も部屋に帰ってないんだ。
あたしも今、ちょうど駅に着いたところでさ」
examples.todokanai: "Just kidding… haha! Did you actually believe that? I actually haven't been in my apartment since Friday. I was just on my way to the station right now."

examples.note: Haruki thinks of a manga cafe behind the station, where other people's presence might let him sleep. The translation relocates it inside the station.
examples.japanese: そうだ、駅裏の漫画喫茶…
examples.todokanai: That's right, the manga cafe in the station…

examples.note: Haruki has reached the station at his destination and says the snow in Paris was so severe he feared he would not arrive that day. 'Here in Paris' leaves him in the wrong city during the phone call.
examples.japanese:
「パリがもう凄い雪でさ、
今日中に着かないかと思ったよ」
examples.todokanai: "It's snowing really hard here in Paris. I didn't think I'd make it by today."

examples.note: The reply comes from a civic orchestra only a five-minute walk away. Todokanai TL omits the striking proximity, a concrete irony after Kazusa's sprawling and unsuccessful international search.
examples.japanese:
アドレスを確認すると、
一番最初にメールを出したけど返事の来なかった、
ここから歩いて五分の市民オケからだった。
examples.todokanai: Checking the address, I noticed it was from the very first orchestra I sent a request to, but never got any response from.

examples.note: Haruki says there are about thirty minutes until the first train. The English says they are thirty minutes away from the station, turning a waiting time into travel distance and obscuring why Mari chooses a taxi.
examples.japanese: 「始発まであと３０分くらいありますけど？」
examples.todokanai: "Aren't we still 30 minutes away from the station?"

examples.note: The user-confirmed reading Arumi is retained in the precise meeting instruction at Arumi Station, without genericizing the destination.
examples.japanese:
『１３時。有海駅前。
ちょっと遠いけどいいかな？』
examples.todokanai: "1 PM, in front of Arumi Station. It's a bit far away, but I hope it's fine."

examples.note: The English correctly names Suetsugucho Station, places it one stop beyond the school's station, and identifies it as the station nearest Setsuna's home.
examples.japanese:
学園の最寄りの駅から一つ先。
ついでに、小木曽の家から最寄りの末次町駅前。
examples.todokanai: We're in front of Suetsugu-chou Station, one station away from school and nearest to Ogiso's house.

dossiers.title: Publishing and workplace process
dossiers.claim: The publishing material contains a recurring technical failure: organizations, job roles, production stages, deadlines, print quantities, and physical manuscript handling are translated as different operations. Because Haruki's profession supplies much of Coda's plot machinery, the errors accumulate into a materially different workplace.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The source distinguishes in-house editorial staff from editorial-production contractors, copy delivered for proofing from a first draft, manuscript submission from publication, proof corrections from still-awaited materials, writing from editing, an initial print run from multiple editions, and personally carrying a manuscript to a printer from purchasing it.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: Editorial-production companies become generic professionals or another publisher; first proofs become first drafts; production tasks are collapsed into passive waiting; a submission deadline becomes a publication date; Haruki becomes a journalist rather than a publishing editor; tens of thousands of copies become tens of thousands of editions; and a last-ditch delivery to the printer becomes buying a manuscript.
dossiers.limits: Natural industry English need not calque every Japanese term, and ordinary workplace jokes may be localized. A finding requires a different organization, responsible worker, production stage, deadline, quantity, or action. The counterexamples show that Todokanai TL can render 編プロ naturally as an editing company and localize a ブラック workplace as a sweatshop without losing the publishing context.

examples.note: 編プロ means editorial-production companies or outsourced editorial staff: Ensemble's chief editor is the only in-house editor, which is why he wants a dedicated subordinate. The translation reads プロ literally as 'professionals,' erasing the staffing arrangement.
examples.japanese:
「あそこ編集長以外全部編プロだもんねぇ。
この前、専任の部下が欲しいってブツブツ言ってた」
examples.todokanai: "Aside from the chief editor, everyone else there is a pro at editing. The chief grumbled earlier about wanting someone to work directly under him."

examples.note: Friday morning is the deadline for Haruki to submit the article, not the publication date for multiple articles. The distinction matters to Kazusa's argument that he still had one or two days of scheduling slack.
examples.japanese:
「…記事の提出期限は金曜朝までだから、
まぁ、１、２日は余裕あったけど」
examples.todokanai: "…All the articles must be published by Friday, though I suppose I had a day or two to spare."

examples.note: Mari's deadline-extending maneuver involves personally carrying the manuscript into the printing company after negotiating with its president. The translation has her buying the manuscript, an unrelated act that makes the publishing workflow nonsensical.
examples.japanese:
例えば、直接印刷所の社長と交渉して、
しかも自分で原稿を持ち込んで、
デッドラインからさらに数時間延ばすという荒業。
examples.todokanai: …Like negotiating with the president of the printing company, buying the manuscript herself, and extending the deadline for several more hours.

examples.note: Matsuoka hands Haruki copy delivered by an outside contractor or freelancer for proofreading. The translation invents another publishing house, changing the production relationship.
examples.japanese:
「これ、外注から上がってきた原稿。
校正頼む、８時までに！」
examples.todokanai: "This is the original draft from another publisher. I'll leave the editing to you, it's due by 8 o'clock!"

examples.note: Haruki plans to continue checking the first proofs on Monday. The translation again calls 初校 a first draft, moving the project backward from proofing to authoring.
examples.japanese:
そして、できれば月曜からちゃんと出勤して、
初校のチェックを進めて…
examples.todokanai: And if possible, I'll be back to work on Monday, and get my first draft checked…

examples.note: The remaining items are correction work, waiting for manuscripts from the editorial production company, supervision or fact-checking, and the editor's afterword. The translation turns tasks into things merely awaited and combines supervisors and editors into authors of multiple postscripts.
examples.japanese:
「あとは修正作業と、編プロの方の原稿待ちと監修と
…それに編集後記だけです」
examples.todokanai: "All that's left now is to wait for the revision and compilation work to finish… as well as the supervisors' and editors' post-scripts."

examples.note: Haruki likens handling interviews, photography, writing, and editing himself to making a doujinshi. The translation invents a one-employee independent studio and loses the self-publishing comparison.
examples.japanese:
もともと最近の雑誌編集の仕事の範囲は広いけど、
今度はインタビューから写真撮影、記事の執筆、
編集までって、まるで同人誌作りの勢いだ。
examples.todokanai: The job of a magazine editor has always been broad, but this time it's interviewing, taking pictures, writing articles, and even editing. It's almost like I'm the only employee in an independent studio.

examples.note: Kazusa stereotypes the publishing industry as tolerant of late mornings because its work runs into the night. The English calls Haruki a journalist, changing his profession and the workplace culture being mocked.
examples.japanese:
「なぁ、そんなに慌てなくても。
出版業界なんて朝は遅刻しても平気なんじゃないのか？
どうせ働き出すのは夜中だろ」
examples.todokanai: "Hey, you don't have to be in such a rush. It's not that big of a deal for a journalist to be late. Most of your work is done at night, anyway."

examples.note: The special issue is a joint project with an editorial-production company, 編プロ, not simply work done 'with professionals.' The English erases the subcontracting structure that makes this Haruki's first commemorative job with direct editorial responsibility.
examples.japanese:
今回の特集号は、編プロと共同とは言え、
俺が直接編集に携わるという意味で、記念すべき初仕事。
examples.todokanai: This current job might be one done along with professionals, but it's also my first job as a direct participant, which ought to be commemorated.

examples.note: Haruki says the initial print run is a censored number of ten-thousands of copies. The English says there will be tens of thousands of 'first editions,' confusing copies with editions and making the publishing-scale objection nonsensical.
examples.japanese:
「待て、待て、待て！
全国の書店で売るんだぞ！？
初版○万部だぞ！？」
examples.todokanai: "Wait, wait, wait! This is going to be selling in bookstores all over the country, you know!? And tens of thousands of first editions, at that!"

examples.note: The gift is a shikishi message board from the Kaiou Graph editorial department. Todokanai TL reads 色紙 literally as colored paper and substitutes a company-like 'Kaiousha' for the named publication, breaking both the physical scene and institutional continuity.
examples.japanese:
彼のベッドの脇には、
開桜グラフ編集部の人たちが贈ってくれた
色紙が飾られている。
examples.todokanai: Beside his bed lies a piece of colored paper, sent by the editorial staff of Kaiousha.

examples.note: Haruki says he will finish the proofreading that night and tells the committee member to secure the printer for the beginning of the week. The English instead delays an unspecified request to the shop until Monday, changing both the booking action and its relation to the deadline.
examples.japanese:
「それは今夜中にやっとくから。
もう週明けで印刷所押さえといて」
examples.todokanai: "It'll be finished tonight. You can make the request to the printing shop this coming Monday."

examples.note: The exploitative ブラック workplace is naturally localized as a sweatshop while the publishing-industry joke and staff exchange remain intact.
examples.japanese:
「ホント期待してるからね小春っち。何しろ最近のウチ、その“ただのアルバイト”が一週間続いたことないんだよねぇ」

「そういうこと言うのやめてよ鈴木さん。それだとウチがまるでブラックみたいじゃん」

「何言ってんだ松岡、ブラックでない出版社が生き残ってる訳ないだろこの出版不況のご時世に」

「木崎さんもさらっと肯定しちゃったらマズいでしょ……」

　しかしまぁ、ここにいる人たちは、社会の先輩として人間ができているのか、それとも心底いい加減なのか、彼女の堅苦しい態度をさらっと受け流して勝手に盛り上がる。
examples.todokanai:
“We’ve got high hopes for you, Kohacchi. Lately, none of our part-timers have stuck around for more than a week…”

“Don’t say stuff like that, Suzuki-san. You’ll make us sound like a sweatshop.”

“What are you talking about, Matsuoka? In times like these, with publications in such a slump, no publishing company could survive without being a sweatshop.”

“Do you have to affirm that so readily, Kizaki-san…?”

But, well, whether it was because they were more experienced members of society as her seniors, or whether they were all just completely irresponsible, the others present let her formal attitude wash right off of them and got swept up in their own lively conversations.

examples.note: The English correctly explains that the magazine normally outsources the issue wholesale to an editing company, preserving 編プロ and the contractor relationship that later passages mistranslate.
examples.japanese:
「あっちの雑誌、本来なら編プロにグロスで
発注してるんだけど、今回のは急遽決まった企画だし、
元ネタ拾ってきたのが私だし…」
examples.todokanai: "Normally their team would be outsourcing this to an editing company, but since we decided on this so suddenly, not to mention the fact I came up with the original idea…"

dossiers.title: Music, performance, and production terminology
dossiers.claim: Across the school-band, professional-concert, theatrical, and rehearsal material, musical terms and actions are repeatedly replaced with different technical propositions. The errors change logistics, instrumentation, rehearsal direction, performance quality, and the collaboration attributed to the performers.
dossiers.sourcePattern: The source distinguishes musical parts from departments, original key from melody, stage allotment from reflection, fingering from rhythm, rough playing from clumsy technique, and ensemble rehearsal from a meeting. Multi-line rehearsal and arrangement sequences resolve performers, restart points, and paired underperformance.
dossiers.todokanaiEffect: The English invents departments and performers, reverses entrusting a voice into replacing one, converts ability into willingness, omits one musician from paired failure, and changes precise rehearsal work into generic meetings or unsupported restart commands.
dossiers.limits: Terminological latitude is permitted where the same musical action survives; 'melody' for tone color remains a bounded non-error. Findings require a different faculty, performer, action, rehearsal stage, or causal account. Held wording is not used as counterevidence.

examples.note: パート means musical parts here. Kazusa says their instrumentation is missing essential parts, not that a nonexistent sound department is understaffed.
examples.japanese:
「今のメンバー構成なら、
誰かがやらなくちゃならない事なの。
絶対的にパートが足りないのよ」
examples.todokanai: "With our current numbers, someone has to take on that role. We absolutely don't have enough people in the sound department."

examples.note: 持ち時間 is the band's allotted stage time. They need more than one song to fill their slot, not because Kazusa has simply given the matter more thought.
examples.japanese:
「持ち時間を考えると、
レパートリー１曲じゃ全然足りないし。
あと２曲、最低でも１曲は」
examples.todokanai: "After giving it some more thought, one song isn't enough for our repertoire. We should have two more songs if possible, or at the very least one more."

examples.note: Chiaki entrusts her voice to Setsuna's recorded singing, an act whose exact singing form the approved note leaves open. The translation says she replaces Setsuna's voice, reversing participation or submission into displacement.
examples.japanese: 雪菜の歌声に、自分の歌声を委ねて。
examples.todokanai: And she replaces Setsuna's singing voice with her own.

examples.note: Youko says Kazusa's playing has become rough, unsettled, or emotionally wild because of her instability. The translation describes the piano itself or her technique as increasingly clumsy.
examples.japanese:
「そのせいでピアノも荒れてる。
正直、今のままの状態じゃコンサートも心許ないわね」
examples.todokanai: "Thanks to that, your piano is getting more clumsy. To be honest, I feel a bit uneasy about holding a concert at this rate."

examples.note: Kazusa asks whether Setsuna can perform the song in its original key. The translation substitutes the unrelated question of whether she can sing its melody.
examples.japanese:
「キーは原曲のまんまで行けるんだよね？
発声練習する？」
examples.todokanai: "You can sing the melody to the song, right? Want to do voice training?"

examples.note: Takeya is reporting Haruki's audacious arrangement instruction: take the bass out of Sound of Destiny and put the keyboard in. The English turns it into something Takeya himself was ordered to do to programmed audio, inventing both the performer and the implementation.
examples.japanese:
「で、『ＳＯＵＮＤ　ＯＦ　ＤＥＳＴＩＮＹ』は、
ベース外してキーボード入れろって…」
examples.todokanai: "And for Sound of Destiny, I was told to delete the bass programming and do the keyboard instead…"

examples.note: Io's complaint is that Kazusa can execute the technically absurd arrangement with ease. “Went along with it” makes the feat one of willing compliance instead of effortless musical ability, breaking the punch line to their exchange about her detestable genius.
examples.japanese:
「それでも簡単にやっちゃうところが、
思いっきり嫌味なんだけどなぁ」
examples.todokanai: "But the fact that she went along with it so easily is what makes it so detestable."

examples.note: The preceding line identifies both Kazusa's bass and Setsuna's vocals. Haruki then says Kazusa was playing roughly and Setsuna's voice was catching; Todokanai TL retains only the vocal hiccups, omitting Kazusa's part of the deliberately paired underperformance.
examples.japanese:
二人とも、視線が泳いでたり、
適当だったり声詰まらせたりして、
じっくり聴いてみれば結構酷いものになってるはずだ。
examples.todokanai: With the way both of their gazes were wandering, and how there were a few hiccups in the singing, it would probably sound pretty bad to anyone listening closely.

examples.note: Haruki and Setsuna can recognize her flawless, precise fingering or handwork. The translation substitutes rhythm, a different musical faculty, in a passage explicitly listing the limited technical features they can assess.
examples.japanese:
疾走するスピード感とか、叩きつける強さとか、
ミスのない正確な指さばきとか、
そういうわかりやすい観点でしか見れない。
examples.todokanai: We can only understand the simple things, like her blistering pace, the force at which she strikes each key, and her accurate sense of rhythm.

examples.note: Dupre orders another repetition, while the preceding instruction has already specified 'from the same place.' 'From the top' adds a restart point that the Japanese does not state; the error is the unsupported restart instruction, not a provable claim that she must restart the entire work.
examples.japanese: 「もう一度！」
examples.todokanai: "From the top!"

examples.note: Dupre attacks Kazusa's piano as spineless or lifeless. Todokanai TL makes Kazusa herself completely useless, changing a severe musical criticism into a broader judgment of the person.
examples.japanese:
「なんだその腑抜けたピアノは…
若手ナンバーワンの成長株だという触れ込みだったが、
とんだ期待はずれだ」
examples.todokanai: "You're completely useless… I heard you were the peerless up and coming pianist, young and full of promise, but this is so far from what I expected."

examples.note: Kazusa has finally reached the first joint ensemble rehearsal, not an introductory meeting. The next lines describe exactly which instruments were allowed to play during that run-through.
examples.japanese:
そして今日、やっとメンバーが揃ったということで、
待望の初合わせ…
examples.todokanai: And today, when my long awaited meeting with the orchestra finally arrived…

examples.note: Although 'melody' is looser than 音色, the English still preserves the absent pianist's intense, gentle, steady sound as the guidance Haruki and Setsuna no longer have.
examples.japanese:
厳しく、そして優しく導いてくれる、
しっかりした音色は、もうここにはない。
examples.todokanai: Her intense, gentle and steady melody is no longer here to guide us.

examples.note: The English preserves Kazusa writing notes on staff paper while her left hand searches the keyboard for sounds to adorn the melody, accurately rendering the act of composing around Haruki's lyrics.
examples.japanese:
『何故だろう、気になっていた』

　ノートの隣に立てかけた五線紙に、鉛筆で音符を書き加えていく。

　左手は相変わらず鍵盤の上を彷徨い、主旋律を飾る音を探している。

　さっきまで、散々笑い飛ばしたその詞に、今は真剣に向き合っている。

　というか元々、詞そのものの出来に文句なんかなかった。

　ちょっと不器用だけど、ちょっと真剣過ぎるけど。

　だからこそ、まっすぐな想いがダイレクトに伝わってきた。

　本音を言えば、少し、グっときていた。

　……ただ、一緒にそれを作った人間の顔が浮かんでしまうから笑えるだけで。
examples.todokanai:
“Couldn’t help but wonder why…”

She scribbled down notations in pencil on the music paper that she had set up next to the notebook.

Her left hand continued roaming over the keys, seeking out sounds to adorn the melody.

Moments ago, she had thoroughly laughed off these lyrics, but now, she faced them seriously.

Really, she hadn’t had any complaint with the execution of the lyrics in the first place.

Even though they were a little clumsy, and a little too earnest.

That was exactly what made the honest feelings in them come across so directly.

To be fully honest, she found herself just a bit moved.

…At the same time, when she pictured the face of the person who had written it, all she could do was laugh.
